Chapter 1 Introduction to Unix In this chapter why biologists work at the command line, and how to choose an operating system how the Unix file system is organized, and how to move around in it the core commands for viewing, finding, copying, moving, and deleting files how to save, combine, and chain command output with redirection and pipes how to slice and summarize data files with grep, cut, sort, uniq, awk, and sed how to automate repetitive work with Bash scripts and loops 1.1 Why the command line? Why not just point and click with a Graphical User Interface (GUI)? GUIs are fine for many things, but they fall short for scientific computing: They’re not good for long sequences of operations that need to be repeated on multiple datasets. They keep no log of what you did and which commands you ran. They’re not conducive to running jobs remotely on a computing cluster. They’re labor-intensive to develop and are generally restricted to a single operating system. Use the command line instead. It’s extremely powerful. It might look like a primitive interface, but it’s not. Learning to work from the command line requires an up-front investment, but the long-term payoff is enormous: It’s an absolute necessity for the big datasets that characterize modern data science. You can automate tasks. You can do, and re-do, and re-do analyses with minimal added effort. It’s easy to record exactly what you did, which minimizes mistakes and makes your work repeatable and easier to troubleshoot. 1.2 Choosing an operating system 1.2.1 macOS Pros Unix is fully and naturally integrated into the operating system. You can still use Microsoft Office, Adobe, and so on. It’s the easiest transition to make, and the choice of many data scientists. It can run most Linux-based software. Cons The hardware is expensive, and the operating system is proprietary. Python no longer comes pre-installed (Apple removed it in 2022), but it’s easy to install with conda or Homebrew. Some bioinformatics programs aren’t yet built for the ARM chips (M1, M2, …) in newer Macs. macOS uses the BSD versions of many Unix commands, which occasionally behave a little differently from the GNU versions on Linux. This book tries to point out the differences that matter (for example, sed -i in Section 1.14). 1.2.2 Linux Pros You can install it as the operating system on any PC. A Linux box is a fraction of the price of a comparably outfitted Mac. It’s compatible with all the important bioinformatics software. It’s open source. Cons It’s open source. You’ve probably never used it, so the learning curve is steeper. Maintaining a Linux box requires some time investment. An aside: Unix vs. Linux. Unix is a family of operating systems that dates back to Bell Labs in the 1970s. macOS is a certified Unix. Linux (“Linus’ Unix,” after its creator Linus Torvalds) is a free, open-source, Unix-like operating system. For the purposes of this course, the commands are nearly identical. The two differ mostly in how they’re developed: Unix Linux proprietary open source targeted development diverse development more consistency between versions less consistency between versions development restrictions no restrictions patches are highly tested not as much beta testing more slowly evolving huge open-source community identifies and fixes problems quickly 1.2.3 Windows Pros None. Cons Too many to name. Windows is not designed for programming and bioinformatics applications. But there are workarounds for running Linux alongside Windows: Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2) runs a real Linux system inside Windows. This is the easiest option for most people (installation guide). VMware runs Linux in a virtual machine (instructions). Log into a remote Linux computer, such as the university’s computing cluster (Chapter 4). Windows 10 and 11 include an ssh command that you can run in PowerShell or Windows Terminal. PuTTY is an older alternative. Boot Linux from a flash drive (e.g., with UNetbootin). You have to restart your computer to switch operating systems. 1.3 The Shell You interact with Unix through a shell, which is: an intermediary between you and the inner workings of the operating system a command interpreter, providing an interface to programs and utilities a programming language, letting you combine utilities in different ways to get things done A shell can be used interactively, accepting commands you type on the keyboard, or non-interactively, reading commands from a file (a script). A shell can: run builtin commands implemented inside the shell itself, such as cd, pwd, and exit; run programs installed elsewhere on the file system, such as the GNU Core Utilities (ls, mv, rm, mkdir, chmod, …). Section 2.1 explains how the shell finds them. There are many different shells. We’ll use Bash or Zsh, which has been the default shell on macOS since 2019. For everything in this course, the two behave the same way. The shell runs inside a text window: on a Mac, that’s the Terminal application. Launch Terminal: Finder > Go > Utilities > Terminal. Add Terminal to your Dock by dragging and dropping it there. You’ll be using it a lot. When the shell is ready for a command, it shows a prompt, often ending in $ or %. Type a command and press Return. Start with these: whoami # what's my user name? echo $SHELL # which shell am I using? echo $HOME # where's my home directory? aja /bin/zsh /Users/aja Anything after a # is a comment; the shell ignores it. This book uses comments to explain what commands do. 1.4 The file system Your computer’s files are organized like a filing cabinet: drawers (folders) hold files and other folders. In Unix, folders are called directories, and they’re organized into a tree that starts at a single root directory, written as a forward slash: /. Figure 1.1: Part of the directory structure on a Mac. Everything branches from the root directory (/). The user aja’s home directory (~) is inside /Users. Modified from Haddock & Dunn, Practical Computing for Biologists. Every user has a home directory where their own files live. On a Mac, it’s /Users/username. The shell uses ~ as shorthand for your home directory. Reading. File not found by Monica Chin (The Verge), on why a generation raised on search bars has never needed to think about directories, and why that’s a problem for scientists. 1.4.1 Paths A path is a written description of a location in the file system. Both directories and files have paths. A path is a series of directory names separated by forward slashes (/). An absolute path gives the complete, unambiguous location of a file, starting from the root. It always starts with a forward slash: /Users/aja/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome/watermelon.fsa The working directory is where you are right now. A relative path describes where a file or directory is relative to some other directory, usually the working directory. If you’re in ~/Desktop, the relative path to watermelon.fsa is: files/data/watermelon_genome/watermelon.fsa A few special names help you write paths: Name Meaning / the root directory (at the start of a path) ~ your home directory . the current (working) directory .. the parent directory, one level up Mac shortcut. You can enter a long path to a file by dragging the file from the Finder and dropping it into the Terminal window. Try it with files/file_types/Don't do this.txt. New rule: no spaces in file names. Look at what happened when you dragged Don't do this.txt into the Terminal: the shell needs backslashes to “escape” the spaces and the apostrophe, because spaces are reserved for separating the parts of a command. Spaces (and other special characters, like parentheses and apostrophes) in file names cause endless trouble at the command line. Instead, use: underscores or dashes: my_file.txt, my-file.txt camelCase (mixed upper and lowercase): myFile.txt dots: my.file.txt 1.4.2 The course files Download files.tgz and move it to your Desktop. A .tgz file is a compressed archive (a “tarball”), similar to a .zip file. Double-click it in the Finder, or extract it at the command line (Section 4.4.3 explains how this works): cd ~/Desktop tar -xzf files.tgz This creates a files directory. We’ll work mostly with the data in files/data: ls covid_genome cowboy_carter.md5sum cowboy_carter.txt fruit.txt letters.txt presidents.csv shaver_etal.csv watermelon_genome The examples in this book assume you’ve extracted files.tgz on your Desktop. If you put it somewhere else, adjust the paths accordingly. Is it an absolute or a relative path? pwd cd changes directory: cd ~/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome # relative to home (~) cd /Users/aja/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome # absolute path cd .. # move up one directory cd ../.. # move up two directories cd # go home cd ~ # also go home cd - # go back to the previous directory echo writes its arguments to the screen (more precisely, to standard output, Section 1.7): echo crazy echo crazy horse crazy crazy horse 1.5.2 clear and exit clear clears the Terminal screen. exit ends your shell session. Exit before you quit. Always exit your session before closing the Terminal window. Not doing so is like unplugging your computer: an unceremonious end to all your programs and processes. Awesome shortcuts. Tab: auto-complete file and command names. Use it constantly; it saves typing and prevents typos. Press it twice to see all the possible completions. ↑ and ↓: scroll through and re-run previous commands. Ctrl+r: search for an old command. history: list your previous commands. open . (Mac only): open the working directory in the Finder. More shortcuts. Ctrl+a: go to the beginning of the command. Ctrl+e: go to the end of the command. Ctrl+u: erase from the cursor to the start of the command. Ctrl+l: clear the screen (same as clear). 1.5.3 Stopping a command: Ctrl+C Sooner or later, you’ll start a command that won’t stop: it’s printing an entire genome to the screen, it’s taking far longer than expected, or it’s just sitting there with no prompt. Don’t close the Terminal window. Instead: Keys What it does Ctrl+C cancel (interrupt) the running command and get your prompt back Ctrl+D signal “end of input” to a command that’s waiting for you to type q quit programs like less and man that take over the whole screen A command with no prompt is often waiting for input. If you forget to give cat or grep a file name, for example, it waits for you to type the input on the keyboard (that’s STDIN, Section 1.7). Exercise 1.2 Type cat with no file name and press Return. Type a few words and press Return. What happens? Press Ctrl+D. Run cat again, and this time get out with Ctrl+C. Run yes, a command that prints y forever. Stop it. 1.5.4 ls: listing directory contents ls lists the contents of a directory. With no arguments, it lists the working directory. Otherwise, give it the path to a directory or file: ls # contents of the working directory ls ~/Desktop # contents of the Desktop ls ~/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome ls ~/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome/watermelon.fsa From here on, most examples are run from inside the watermelon_genome directory: cd ~/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome ls aa mt_genomes nt watermelon.fsa watermelon.gbf watermelon.gff Most Unix commands take options (also called flags or arguments) that modify their behavior. Options start with a dash. Useful options for ls: Option Effect -a list all contents, including hidden files -l long format -h human-readable file sizes (with -l) -t sort by time modified, most recent first -S sort by file Size, largest first Single-letter options can be given separately or combined. These are all the same command: ls -a -l ls -al ls -la Add more options to sort by size and show human-readable sizes: ls -alSh total 2000 -rw------- 1 aja staff 609K Jan 4 2019 watermelon.gbf -rw------- 1 aja staff 371K Aug 21 2023 watermelon.fsa -rw------- 1 aja staff 16K Jan 4 2019 watermelon.gff drwxr-xr-x 62 aja staff 1.9K Nov 2 18:15 nt drwxr-xr-x 41 aja staff 1.3K Nov 2 18:15 aa drwxr-xr-x 25 aja staff 800B Nov 2 18:15 mt_genomes drwxr-xr-x 10 aja staff 320B Nov 2 18:15 .. drwxr-xr-x 8 aja staff 256B Nov 2 18:15 . Files whose names start with a dot (like .DS_Store) are hidden files; plain ls doesn’t show them. . and .. are links to the current and parent directories. 1.5.5 Reading ls -l output Each line of a long listing describes one file or directory: -rw------- 1 aja staff 371K Aug 21 2023 watermelon.fsa Field Meaning - file type: - for a file, d for a directory, l for a link rw------- permissions for the user, group, and others (Section 1.15.3) 1 number of links (for directories, roughly how many items inside) aja the file’s owner staff the owner’s user group 371K file size Aug 21 2023 date and time last modified watermelon.fsa file name 1.5.6 Wildcards A wildcard stands in for other characters in a file name. The most important one is *, the wildest of all wildcards: it matches any number of any characters (except a slash). ls *.gff # every file that ends in .gff ls nt/cox* # every file in nt/ that starts with cox watermelon.gff nt/cox1.fasta nt/cox2.fasta nt/cox3.fasta ls -l */nad1* # nad1 files in any subdirectory -rw------- 1 aja staff 350 Jan 4 2019 aa/nad1.fasta -rw------- 1 aja staff 995 Jan 4 2019 nt/nad1.fasta Two less common wildcards are sometimes handy: ? matches exactly one character, and [...] matches any one of the characters inside the brackets. ls nt/atp?.fasta # atp followed by exactly one character ls nt/cox[13].fasta # cox1 or cox3 nt/atp1.fasta nt/atp4.fasta nt/atp6.fasta nt/atp8.fasta nt/atp9.fasta nt/cox1.fasta nt/cox3.fasta Exercise 1.3 From inside watermelon_genome: Show a long listing of all the atp genes in the aa directory. Its structure is find where tests: Test Finds -name 'pattern' names matching a pattern (wildcards allowed) -iname 'pattern' the same, but ignoring upper/lowercase -type f files only -type d directories only -size +500k files bigger than 500 kilobytes (M for megabytes) -mtime -7 files modified in the last 7 days find . -name '*.csv' # all CSV files, starting here (.) ./presidents.csv ./shaver_etal.csv find . -type d # all directories . ./watermelon_genome ./watermelon_genome/nt ./watermelon_genome/mt_genomes ./watermelon_genome/aa ./covid_genome find watermelon_genome -name 'nad1*' # every nad1 file under watermelon_genome watermelon_genome/nt/nad1.fasta watermelon_genome/aa/nad1.fasta find . -type f -size +700k # big files ./watermelon_genome/mt_genomes/vitis_vinifera.fasta ./watermelon_genome/mt_genomes/cucurbita_pepo.fasta Put the pattern in quotes. The first is the manual pages, which describe a program’s usage and all its options: man ls You navigate and search a man page just like a file in less; press q to exit. Man pages are usually straightforward, but not always. The second way is to search the web, which is often faster. Getting help from AI assistants. Chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot are good at explaining what an unfamiliar command does and at suggesting commands for a task. Use them, but: Ask for an explanation of every part of a command you don’t understand, and check it against the man page. Test suggested commands on copies of your data (in /tmp, for example) before running them on the real thing. Be especially careful with anything that uses rm, mv, >, sed -i, or a loop over many files. You’re responsible for what you run, not the chatbot. What if we want to save them? 1.7.1 Redirecting STDOUT Use > to send STDOUT to a file instead of the screen: ls -al > contents.txt cat nt/nad*.fasta > nad_genes.fasta Use >> to append to the end of an existing file: echo 'directory listing' > dir.out ls -al >> dir.out > overwrites. If you redirect with a single > to a file that already exists, the shell completely overwrites it, without warning. End files with a newline. Before combining lots of files with cat, make sure each file ends with a newline character. Otherwise, the first line of one file will be glued onto the last line of the file before it. Here, one file exists and the other doesn’t, so we get both STDOUT and STDERR: ls -l watermelon.fsa nada.txt ls: nada.txt: No such file or directory -rw------- 1 aja staff 379432 Aug 21 2023 watermelon.fsa ls -l watermelon.fsa nada.txt > listing.txt 2> err.txt # STDOUT and STDERR to separate files ls -l watermelon.fsa nada.txt 2> err.txt # STDOUT to the screen, STDERR to a file ls -l watermelon.fsa nada.txt 2>> err.txt # append STDERR to a file Sometimes you want to throw output away entirely. /dev/null is a “black hole”: anything redirected there disappears. ls -l watermelon.fsa nada.txt > /dev/null # discard STDOUT; only the error is shown ls: nada.txt: No such file or directory This is handy for programs that print huge amounts of output you don’t need, while you save their error messages to a log file. Compare a GFF file saved as plain text with the same content saved as a Word document: cd ~/Desktop/files/file_types less -S watermelon.gff less -S watermelon.gff.docx The file command tells you what kind of file you have: file * Don't do this.txt: ASCII text watermelon_genes.mac.txt: ASCII text, with CR line terminators watermelon.gff: ASCII text, with very long lines (616) watermelon.gff.docx: Microsoft Word 2007+ watermelon.mac.gff: ASCII text, with very long lines (648), with CR line terminators Free alternatives to Microsoft Office, such as LibreOffice, tend not to introduce weirdness into files the way Microsoft products do. 1.8.2 Line breaks matter Different operating systems mark the end of a line with different invisible characters: Character(s) Name Used by \n newline (line feed, LF) Unix, Linux, and macOS \r\n carriage return + newline Windows \r carriage return (CR) classic Mac OS (before 2001) Today, the line breaks you’ll run into most often are Windows-style \r\n, in files from Windows users or exported from Windows programs. Old-style Mac \r line breaks still turn up in files from older software. Notice the CR line terminators in the file output above, and look at what wc -l (which counts \n characters) thinks of those files: wc -l watermelon.gff watermelon.mac.gff 144 watermelon.gff 0 watermelon.mac.gff 144 total Look at the two versions yourself: less watermelon.gff less watermelon.mac.gff less shows the carriage returns as ^M, and the whole file appears as one long line. If a program can’t read a file, or dies without running, check the line breaks. Many text editors can change line breaks with “Save As,” and the tr (translate characters) command can fix them at the command line: tr '\r' '\n' < watermelon.mac.gff > watermelon.fixed.gff # old Mac: replace \r with \n wc -l watermelon.fixed.gff 144 watermelon.fixed.gff tr -d '\r' < windows_file.txt > fixed_file.txt # Windows: delete the \r tr only reads from STDIN, so the input file is redirected in with <. Later in the course, we’ll also write a Python script to fix line breaks. 1.8.3 Text editors You’ll need a good text editor for writing scripts and editing data files: nano (“nano’s another editor”): quick and dirty text editing right in the Terminal. Run nano filename; the commands are listed at the bottom of the screen (^ means Ctrl). Visual Studio Code: free and excellent for programming. This is what we’ll use in class. BBEdit (Mac): an all-around workhorse for text editing, with good features for programming. Open files from the command line with bbedit filename. 1.8.4 Fonts Get used to reading and writing code in a monospace (fixed-width) font, such as Courier, Menlo, or Monaco, where every character takes up the same amount of space. In a proportional font, characters have different widths, so things that should line up don’t, which matters a lot for sequence alignments: Proportional Monospace AAAccgGTT|||||||||AAG--TAAC AAAccgGTT|||||||||AAG--TAAC Exercise 1.10 Use nano to create a file called my_genes.txt listing three of your favorite genes, one per line. Why?) 1.9 Managing files and directories Really important warnings. Unix commands are permanent. There is no Trash or Recycle Bin. There are usually no warnings. If you overwrite a file, it’s gone forever. If you delete a file, it’s gone forever. Use the -i flag with cp, mv, and rm until you’re comfortable. It makes the command ask for confirmation before overwriting or removing anything. Back up your data. If you don’t, and you lose it, it’s your own fault. Use Box, Google Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox. Mac users: also use Time Machine. Have at least two backups of your important files. These backups should be in different physical locations. Make copies of your files before doing something drastic. Make dummy files and folders and test your commands on those first. The /tmp directory is a good place for this. You can do real and permanent damage with the commands you learn in this course. 1.9.1 Copying and moving: cp and mv cp copies a file: cp source target. cd ~/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome cp watermelon.fsa copy.fasta # copy within the same directory cp watermelon.fsa ~/Documents/copy.fasta # copy to another directory cd cp ~/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome/copy.fasta ~/Documents/second_copy.fasta cp ~/Desktop/files/data/watermelon_genome/copy.fasta ~/Documents # keep the same name To copy a directory and everything in it, add -r (recursive). Without it, cp refuses to copy directories: cp -r nt nt_backup # copy the nt directory and all its files cp -r nt ~/Desktop/ # copy it to the Desktop, keeping its name mv moves or renames a file or directory: mv source target. Unlike cp, it works on directories without -r. mv copy.fasta junk.dat # rename a file mv junk.dat /tmp/tmp.fas # move and rename mv watermelon_genome /tmp # move a whole directory mv /tmp/watermelon_genome . # move it back here (.) 1.9.2 Making directories: mkdir mkdir makes one or more directories: mkdir cowgirl mkdir cowgirl in the sand # makes four directories: cowgirl, in, the, sand ls -al What happened with the second command, and why? (Remember the rule about spaces in file names.) mkdir -p (parents) creates a whole path of nested directories at once, and doesn’t complain if a directory already exists: mkdir -p project/data/raw mkdir -p project/results find project project project/results project/data project/data/raw 1.9.3 Deleting: rm and rmdir rm removes files: rm ~/Documents/second_copy.fasta rm ~/Documents/copy.fasta rmdir removes directories, but only empty ones, which makes it of limited use. To remove a directory and everything in it, use rm -r (recursive): rm -r cowgirl # removes all the files in cowgirl, then cowgirl itself rm -r is dangerous. It’s a very dangerous command that you will use all the time. Double-check what you’re deleting before you press Return, and consider using rm -ri until you’re comfortable. 1.9.4 Links: ln ln -s makes a symbolic link to a file or directory, similar to an alias or shortcut: ln -s filename # link has the same name as the file ln -s filename link-name # link has a new name ln -s directory link-name # links work for directories, too Opening or editing the link opens or edits the actual file being linked to. You can link to links. Links keep you from having lots of copies of the same file sitting around, which becomes a real problem when you start editing them. (Which one is the real FINAL_ANALYSES?) Use unlink or rm to remove a link. Special characters. grep treats patterns as regular expressions (more on these later), where characters like ., (, and * have special meanings. For that, you’ll need awk (Section 1.13). 1.10.5 uniq: removing duplicates uniq removes consecutive duplicate lines, keeping one of each: Option Effect -c show a count of occurrences next to each line -d show only duplicated lines cat letters.txt A A B C B C C C uniq letters.txt A B C B C Why are there still two Bs and two Cs? Because uniq only collapses duplicates that are next to each other. To get truly unique values, sort first: sort letters.txt | uniq A B C sort letters.txt | uniq -c # count occurrences of each line 2 A 2 B 4 C Can you get the unique values with sort alone? (Check man sort.) Answer Yes: sort -u (unique) removes duplicates as it sorts, printing one copy of each distinct line. It gives the same result as sort | uniq in one step: sort -u letters.txt A B C Combined with -k, -u looks only at the key column. Lines count as duplicates if their keys match, even if the rest of the line is different: sort -u -k2,2 fruit.txt # one line for each kind of fruit 1 apple OH 2 pear OH sort kept one line for each fruit and threw away the others. That’s handy for listing the distinct values in a column, but remember that the other lines are gone. Use -k2,2, not -k2, with -u. -k2 means “from column 2 to the end of the line”, and -k2,2 means “column 2 only”. Every line of fruit.txt is different from column 2 to the end, so sort -u -k2 fruit.txt doesn’t remove anything. Use uniq when you need one of its options, like counting with -c. 1.10.6 column: viewing tables column -t lines up the columns of a file into a clean, readable table: column -t fruit.txt 1 apple OH 2 pear OH 3 pear IL 4 apple FL 5 pear FL 6 apple MI Try column -t watermelon_genome/watermelon.gff | less -S. 1.10.7 diff: comparing files diff compares two files line by line and prints the lines that differ. No output means the files are identical: diff watermelon_genome/watermelon.gff ../file_types/watermelon.gff Here’s what it looks like when files differ: sort letters.txt > letters_sorted.txt diff letters.txt letters_sorted.txt 4d3 < C 8a8 > C Lines starting with < come from the first file, and lines starting with > come from the second. The lines like 4d3 describe how to turn the first file into the second: 4d3 means “delete line 4 of the first file,” and 8a8 means “add this after line 8.” You’ll also see c for changed lines. Most of the time, you only care whether two files differ, and which lines. 1.11 Pipes A pipe, |, sends the STDOUT of one command to the STDIN of the next: command [options] filename | command [options] | command [options] The first command reads an input file; each subsequent command takes the output of the previous command as its input. There’s no limit to the number of pipes in a command. Pipes are amazing. For example, how many features of each type are in the watermelon mitochondrial genome? cut -f 3 watermelon.gff | sort | uniq -c 64 CDS 20 intron 37 misc_feature 2 repeat_region 3 rRNA 18 tRNA Build pipelines one step at a time: run the first command, check its output, then add the next | and command, and so on. The value can be virtually anything: a number, a file name, a sentence. As the name suggests, the value can vary, which is what makes variables so flexible and useful. You’ve already used two variables that the shell sets for you: $HOME and $SHELL. In Bash, there’s no $ when you assign a value to a variable, but you need a $ when you use it: gene=cox1 echo $gene echo "The gene is $gene" cox1 The gene is cox1 There must be no spaces around the =. With spaces, the shell thinks gene is a command: gene = cox1 bash: gene: command not found When a variable is followed directly by other characters, wrap its name in braces, ${...}, so the shell knows where the name ends: gene=cox1 echo $gene_aligned.fasta # looks for a variable named "gene_aligned"; there isn't one echo ${gene}_aligned.fasta # braces mark the end of the name .fasta cox1_aligned.fasta 1.12.2 Quotes and special characters Many characters mean something special to the shell: spaces separate arguments, * is a wildcard, $ starts a variable, > and | redirect, # starts a comment, and parentheses do things we won’t cover here. Quoting turns off those special meanings. Quoting Effect 'single' everything inside is literal; nothing is special "double" everything is literal except $ (variables still work) \ backslash: makes the one character right after it literal echo '$HOME' # single quotes: literal echo "$HOME" # double quotes: the variable is replaced with its value echo *.csv # no quotes: the shell expands the wildcard echo "*.csv" # quotes: just the characters * . c s v $HOME /Users/aja presidents.csv shaver_etal.csv *.csv Quoting matters for file names with special characters. A few of the tRNA files in nt have parentheses in their names, which confuse the shell: ls nt/trnN(GTT)-cp.fasta bash: -c: line 0: syntax error near unexpected token `(' bash: -c: line 0: `ls nt/trnN(GTT)-cp.fasta' Quoting the name, or escaping each special character with a backslash, fixes it. (Tab completion adds the backslashes for you.) ls 'nt/trnN(GTT)-cp.fasta' ls nt/trnN\(GTT\)-cp.fasta nt/trnN(GTT)-cp.fasta nt/trnN(GTT)-cp.fasta Rules of thumb: Put patterns and code meant for another program in single quotes: grep '>', find . -name '*.fasta', and everything you give to awk and sed (next sections). Put text containing variables in double quotes: echo "Processing $file". Better yet, don’t create file names that need quoting. Exercise 1.16 Predict the output of each command, then run it to check. species=watermelon echo $species echo '$species' echo "$species" echo "My favorite is the $species." echo "$species_genome.fasta" echo "${species}_genome.fasta" echo "Files: *.fasta" echo Files: *.fasta 1.13 awk: working with columns awk is a small programming language for working with text that’s organized into columns, which describes most biological data files. Where cut can only pull out columns, awk can also filter rows based on what’s in a column, rearrange columns, do math with them, and summarize them. You can do a lot with a handful of patterns, which is all we’ll cover here. 1.13.1 How awk reads a file awk reads a file one line at a time. For each line, it: splits the line into fields (columns); stores the fields in numbered variables: $1 is the first field, $2 the second, and so on; $0 is the whole line; checks the line against your pattern, and if it matches, runs your action. Every awk command has this structure: awk 'pattern { action }' filename The whole program goes in single quotes, so the shell doesn’t interpret the $s. The pattern decides which lines to act on. If you leave it out, the action runs on every line. The action, in braces, says what to do with each matching line. If you leave it out, awk prints the whole line. awk also keeps track of a few useful built-in variables: Variable Meaning $0 the whole current line $1, $2, … the first, second, … field of the current line NR Number of the current Record (line), starting at 1 NF Number of Fields on the current line 1.13.2 Printing columns (the action) With only an action, awk runs it on every line. print prints whatever you list, separated by commas: awk '{ print $2 }' fruit.txt # just the fruit apple pear pear apple pear apple Unlike cut, awk can put columns in any order: awk '{ print $3, $2 }' fruit.txt # state, then fruit OH apple OH pear IL pear FL apple FL pear MI apple You can mix in your own text (in double quotes) and the built-in variables: awk '{ print "line " NR ": " $2 " from " $3 }' fruit.txt line 1: apple from OH line 2: pear from OH line 3: pear from IL line 4: apple from FL line 5: pear from FL line 6: apple from MI 1.13.3 Filtering rows (the pattern) With only a pattern, awk prints the lines that match. A pattern is usually a comparison: awk '$1 > 3' fruit.txt # rows where column 1 is greater than 3 4 apple FL 5 pear FL 6 apple MI awk '$3 == "OH"' fruit.txt # rows where column 3 is exactly OH 1 apple OH 2 pear OH These are the comparisons you can use: Operator Meaning Example == equal to $3 == "OH" != not equal to $2 != "apple" >, < greater than, less than $1 > 3 >=, <= greater/less than or equal to $6 >= 1000 ~ contains a match to a pattern $9 ~ /nad/ !~ does not contain the pattern $9 !~ /nad/ && and: both must be true $1 > 3 && $2 == "apple" \|\| or: either can be true $3 == "OH" \|\| $3 == "MI" Text values go in double quotes ("OH"); numbers don’t. Note that a comparison uses == (two equals signs). A single = assigns a value, which is a common and confusing mistake. awk '$2 == "apple" && $1 > 3' fruit.txt 4 apple FL 6 apple MI A pattern like /apple/, between slashes, matches lines that contain apple anywhere, just like grep: awk '/apple/' fruit.txt 1 apple OH 4 apple FL 6 apple MI 1.13.4 Both together Put a pattern and an action together to print selected columns from selected rows: awk '$2 == "pear" { print $3 }' fruit.txt # states where we have pears OH IL FL 1.13.5 Tabs and commas: setting the field separator By default, awk splits fields on any run of spaces or tabs. That’s a problem for watermelon.gff, which is tab-delimited and has a space inside column 1 (Citrullus lanatus). Watch what happens: awk '{ print $1 }' watermelon.gff | head -n 2 # wrong: splits on the space Citrullus Citrullus Use -F to set the Field separator. For tab-delimited files (GFF, BLAST output, and most bioinformatics tables), use -F '\t'. For CSV files, use -F ','. awk -F '\t' '{ print $1 }' watermelon.gff | head -n 2 # right Citrullus lanatus Citrullus lanatus Always use -F '\t' for GFF and other tab-delimited files. Otherwise, any spaces inside a column will silently shift the column numbers, and you’ll get wrong answers without any error message. By default, print separates its output with a space. To keep the output tab-delimited, set the Output Field Separator with -v OFS='\t': awk -F '\t' -v OFS='\t' '$3 == "tRNA" && $7 == "-" { print $4, $5, $9 }' watermelon.gff | head -n 3 44457 44528 Gene trnQ(TTG)-1 ; COLOR red ; type exon 45547 45618 Gene trnG(GCC)-1 ; COLOR red ; type exon 50761 50833 Gene trnM(CAT)-cp ; COLOR red ; type exon That one command answers the “tRNAs on the minus strand” question from the Pipes exercises: rows where column 3 is tRNA and column 7 is -, printing the start, end, and details. 1.13.6 Doing math awk can calculate with columns. In watermelon.gff, column 6 is each feature’s length, but you can also calculate it from the coordinates: awk -F '\t' -v OFS='\t' '$3 == "intron" { print $4, $5, $5 - $4 + 1 }' watermelon.gff | head -n 3 727 1693 967 30629 32108 1480 33007 34731 1725 1.13.7 Summarizing: END To add up a column, keep a running total in a variable of your own, then print it at the end. END is a special pattern that matches once, after the last line has been read: awk -F '\t' '$3 == "CDS" { total = total + $6 } END { print total }' watermelon.gff 32442 Read that as: “for every CDS row, add column 6 to total; when you’re done with the file, print total.” Variables you make up (like total) don’t need a $, and they start at 0. You can calculate an average by also counting the rows: awk -F '\t' '$3 == "CDS" { total = total + $6; n = n + 1 } END { print "mean CDS length:", total / n }' watermelon.gff mean CDS length: 506.906 (Two statements inside one set of braces are separated by a semicolon.) 1.13.8 awk cheat sheet I want to… Command print column 2 awk '{ print $2 }' file print columns 3 and 1, in that order awk '{ print $3, $1 }' file print rows where column 3 is OH awk '$3 == "OH"' file print rows where column 1 is more than 3 awk '$1 > 3' file print rows containing apple anywhere awk '/apple/' file print rows where column 9 contains nad awk -F '\t' '$9 ~ /nad/' file print column 9 for rows where column 3 is tRNA awk -F '\t' '$3 == "tRNA" { print $9 }' file work with a tab-delimited file awk -F '\t' ... work with a CSV file awk -F ',' ... keep output tab-delimited awk -F '\t' -v OFS='\t' ... skip the header line awk 'NR > 1' file sum column 6 awk '{ s = s + $6 } END { print s }' file count lines (like wc -l) awk 'END { print NR }' file Exercise 1.17 Use awk for each of these. It can do many things, but you’ll use it mostly for one: find and replace. 1.14.1 Substitution: s/old/new/ The substitution command has this form: sed 's/old/new/' filename s means substitute. old is the text to find; new is what to replace it with. The /s separate the parts. Like awk, the command goes in single quotes. sed 's/pear/banana/' fruit.txt 1 apple OH 2 banana OH 3 banana IL 4 apple FL 5 banana FL 6 apple MI sed prints the edited text to STDOUT. The original file is unchanged. To keep the result, redirect it to a new file: sed 's/pear/banana/' fruit.txt > fruit_banana.txt diff fruit.txt fruit_banana.txt 2,3c2,3 < 2 pear OH < 3 pear IL --- > 2 banana OH > 3 banana IL 5c5 < 5 pear FL --- > 5 banana FL 1.14.2 Replacing every match: g By default, sed replaces only the first match on each line. Add g (global) at the end to replace every match: echo "pear pear pear" | sed 's/pear/kiwi/' echo "pear pear pear" | sed 's/pear/kiwi/g' kiwi pear pear kiwi kiwi kiwi 1.14.3 Practical examples Rename the sequences in a FASTA file by changing their header lines: sed 's/>Citrullus_/>watermelon_/' nt/atp9.fasta | head -n 1 >watermelon_atp9 ^ and $ are special in the “find” part: ^ matches the start of a line and $ matches the end. They let you add text to the start or end of every line: sed 's/^/fruit_/' fruit.txt | head -n 2 # add text to the start of each line fruit_1 apple OH fruit_2 pear OH sed 's/$/ USA/' fruit.txt | head -n 2 # add text to the end of each line 1 apple OH USA 2 pear OH USA Replace with nothing to delete text: sed 's/ OH$//' fruit.txt # delete " OH" at the end of a line 1 apple 2 pear 3 pear IL 4 apple FL 5 pear FL 6 apple MI If your text contains slashes (like file paths), use a different separator, such as |. sed uses whatever character follows the s: echo "/Users/aja/Desktop/data" | sed 's|/Users/aja|~|' ~/Desktop/data 1.14.4 Deleting and printing lines Besides substituting, two other sed commands are worth knowing: /pattern/d deletes lines that match a pattern. -n 'X,Yp' prints only lines X through Y. sed '/^>/d' nt/atp9.fasta | cut -c 1-60 # delete header lines: sequence only ATGTTAGAAGGTGCAAAATCAATGGGTGCCGGAGCTGCTACAATTGCTTCAGCGGGAGCT sed -n '2,4p' fruit.txt # print lines 2 through 4 2 pear OH 3 pear IL 4 apple FL sed '1d' fruit.txt # delete line 1 2 pear OH 3 pear IL 4 apple FL 5 pear FL 6 apple MI 1.14.5 Editing a file in place: -i To change the file itself instead of printing the result, use -i (in place). This is one place where macOS and Linux differ. The safest habit, which works on both, is to give -i a file extension. sed saves a backup of the original with that extension before editing: sed -i.bak 's/apple/APPLE/' fruit.txt head -n 1 fruit.txt fruit.txt.bak ==> fruit.txt <== 1 APPLE OH ==> fruit.txt.bak <== 1 apple OH Once you’ve checked the result, delete the .bak file. Never redirect sed output back to the same file. sed 's/a/b/' file.txt > file.txt does not edit the file. The shell empties file.txt (to get it ready for the output) before sed reads it, so you end up with an empty file. This is true for every command, not just sed. Use -i.bak, or write to a new file. 1.14.6 sed cheat sheet I want to… Command replace the first old on each line with new sed 's/old/new/' file replace every old with new sed 's/old/new/g' file delete every old sed 's/old//g' file add text to the start of every line sed 's/^/text/' file add text to the end of every line sed 's/$/text/' file replace text containing slashes sed 's\|/old/path\|/new/path\|' file delete lines containing pattern sed '/pattern/d' file delete the first line sed '1d' file print only lines 10 through 20 sed -n '10,20p' file edit the file itself, keeping a backup sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file Exercise 1.18 Print fruit.txt with every pear replaced by PEAR. Print lines 50 through 55 of watermelon.gff. Make a copy of fruit.txt, then use sed -i.bak to change OH to Ohio in the copy. Compare the copy to its backup with diff. 1.15 Bash scripts 1.15.1 Running several commands There are lots of ways to run multiple commands in sequence: pipes, as above; commands separated by semicolons; commands joined by && or ||; Bash scripts. Syntax Meaning cmd1; cmd2 run cmd1, then run cmd2 no matter what cmd1 && cmd2 run cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeded cmd1 \|\| cmd2 run cmd2 only if cmd1 failed Every command reports whether it succeeded when it finishes. && lets you make the next step depend on the previous one: ls nada.txt; echo "this runs anyway" ls: nada.txt: No such file or directory this runs anyway ls nada.txt && echo "this only runs if ls worked" ls: nada.txt: No such file or directory ls nada.txt || echo "ls failed, so this runs" ls: nada.txt: No such file or directory ls failed, so this runs A common use is to only move on if a step worked: mkdir -p results && cd results 1.15.2 Writing a script A Bash script is an executable text file containing a set of commands. In addition to automating your tasks, Bash scripts provide a permanent record of what you did. #!/bin/bash command1 command2 command3 The first line, #!/bin/bash, is the shebang (from the # “hash” and the ! “bang”). It tells the operating system to run the rest of the file with /bin/bash. After that comes a series of commands: Unix commands, other scripts, or programs, run in order from top to bottom. By convention, Bash scripts end in .sh. The file must be executable (next section). Then run it from the command line by giving its path: ./bash_script1.sh The ./ means “in the current directory.” By default, the shell only looks for programs in a specific set of directories, so you have to tell it where your script is. 1.15.3 File permissions: chmod Every file has three kinds of permissions: read: view the file write: change the file execute: run the file as a program Each kind of permission is set separately for three sets of people: the user who owns the file, the user’s group, and all other users. That’s what the first column of ls -l shows: -rwxr-xr-- └┬┘└┬┘└┬┘ │ │ └── other: read only │ └───── group: read and execute └──────── user: read, write, and execute chmod (change mode) changes permissions. The syntax is chmod [who][+/-][what] filename, with no spaces in the middle part: chmod u+x bash_script1.sh # give the user (you) permission to execute chmod u+x *.sh # ...for all your .sh files chmod ugo-x *.* # remove execute permission from everyone chmod ugo+rwx * # give everyone permission to do everything Be careful with permissions. Don’t assign execute permissions willy-nilly, and think twice before giving everyone write permission. Change the script so that it saves the listing to a file instead of printing it to the screen. Run it again and check the file. Write a script, summarize_gff.sh, that prints the number of features of each type in watermelon.gff (Section 1.11), followed by the total length of all CDS features (Section 1.13). Use echo to label each part of the output. 1.16 Loops A loop is a control structure that repeats the same command(s), for example, on many files. Loops let you: change the file suffix of every file in a directory; run some program or analysis on lots of files; generate a list of commands for a Bash script. 1.16.1 for loops A Bash for loop has this structure: for VARIABLE in LIST do command1 on $VARIABLE command2 on $VARIABLE commandN on $VARIABLE done for VARIABLE in LIST names your variable (Section 1.12.1) and the list of values to iterate over. Each time through the loop, the variable takes the next value in the list. do starts the list of commands to run each time through. done closes the loop. for number in 1 2 3 4 do echo "This is iteration $number" done This is iteration 1 This is iteration 2 This is iteration 3 This is iteration 4 The list is often a set of files, given with a wildcard: for fasta in atp*.fasta do echo "$fasta has $(grep -c '>' $fasta) sequence(s)" done atp1.fasta has 1 sequence(s) atp4.fasta has 1 sequence(s) atp6.fasta has 1 sequence(s) atp8.fasta has 1 sequence(s) atp9.fasta has 1 sequence(s) ($(command) runs command and substitutes its output in place.) You can also write a loop on a single line, separating its parts with semicolons. This is handy at the command line: for fasta in *.fasta; do echo $fasta; done 1.16.2 Changing file names in a loop A common task is to run a program on many files and name each output file after its input. Bash’s parameter expansion trims text from the start or end of a variable’s value: Syntax Removes ${var%pattern} the shortest match to pattern from the end ${var%%pattern} the longest match to pattern from the end ${var#pattern} the shortest match to pattern from the start ${var##pattern} the longest match to pattern from the start To remember which is which: on a US keyboard, # (Shift+3) is to the left of % (Shift+5), so # trims from the left (start), and % trims from the right (end). Removing something from the end is the most common case: swapping one file extension for another. fasta=nad1.fasta echo ${fasta%.fasta} echo ${fasta%.fasta}.phy nad1 nad1.phy Removing something from the front works the same way with #. Say your sequencing center added a prefix to every file name: file=run42_sampleA.fastq echo ${file#run42_} sampleA.fastq The pattern can include wildcards. That’s when “shortest” and “longest” matter: file=run42_sampleA_R1.fastq.gz echo ${file#*_} # shortest match to "anything then _" from the start echo ${file##*_} # longest match: everything up to the LAST _ echo ${file%.*} # shortest match to ".anything" from the end echo ${file%%.*} # longest match: everything from the FIRST . sampleA_R1.fastq.gz R1.fastq.gz run42_sampleA_R1.fastq run42_sampleA_R1 A handy use of ## and % is splitting a path into a file name and a directory: path=watermelon_genome/nt/atp1.fasta echo ${path##*/} # remove everything up to the last /: the file name echo ${path%/*} # remove the last / and everything after: the directory atp1.fasta watermelon_genome/nt So this loop converts every FASTA file in a directory to PHYLIP format with a (hypothetical) script fasta2phylip.py, writing nad1.phy for nad1.fasta, and so on: for fasta in *.fasta do fasta2phylip.py $fasta > ${fasta%.fasta}.phy done And this loop removes the prefix run42_ from every file that has it: for file in run42_* do mv $file ${file#run42_} done Test before you run. Put echo in front of the command inside a loop to print what the loop would do, without doing it. When the commands look right, remove the echo. for file in run42_sampleA.fastq run42_sampleB.fastq run42_sampleC.fastq do echo mv $file ${file#run42_} done mv run42_sampleA.fastq sampleA.fastq mv run42_sampleB.fastq sampleB.fastq mv run42_sampleC.fastq sampleC.fastq Exercise 1.20 Do these in a copy of the nt directory (cp -r nt nt_copy). Write a loop that prints the name of each nad file and the number of lines in it. Write a loop that renames every .fasta file to end in .fa instead. Test it with echo first. Write a loop that adds the prefix Clanatus_ to the name of every .fa file. Then write another loop that removes it. Write a loop that makes a copy of each atp file with the sequence only (no header line), named like atp1.seq. (Hint: Section 1.14.) Put your answer to question 4 in a Bash script and run it. 1.17 Command summary Command What it does pwd print the working directory cd change directory ls list directory contents find search for files below a directory echo print text to STDOUT clear, exit clear the screen; end the session cat print and concatenate files head, tail show the first or last lines of a file less page through a file man show a command’s manual page file identify a file’s type tr translate or delete characters nano edit a file in the Terminal cp, cp -r copy files; copy directories mv move or rename mkdir, mkdir -p make a directory; make nested directories rm, rm -r remove files; remove directories and contents ln -s make a symbolic link du -sh, df -h disk space used; disk space free wc count lines, words, and characters sort sort lines grep find lines matching a pattern cut extract columns or characters uniq remove consecutive duplicate lines column -t format columns as a table diff compare two files awk filter, rearrange, and summarize columns sed find and replace; delete or print lines chmod change file permissions Symbol or key Meaning ~ your home directory ., .. the current directory; the parent directory *, ?, [...] wildcards: any characters; one character; one of these characters >, >> redirect STDOUT to a file (overwrite; append) 2> redirect STDERR to a file < redirect a file to STDIN \| pipe STDOUT to the next command ;, &&, \|\| run next command: always; if success; if failure $name, ${name} the value of variable name '...', "...", \ quoting: all literal; literal except $; next character literal ${v%x}, ${v#x} remove x from the end; from the start # comment; or, in #!, the shebang Tab auto-complete Ctrl+C cancel the running command Ctrl+D end of input

Chapter 2 Tailoring your shell In this chapter where the programs you run actually live, and how the shell finds them (your $PATH) how to make your own scripts runnable from anywhere the shell’s configuration files (.zshrc, .bashrc, and .bash_profile), and which one to use how to make aliases (keyboard shortcuts) for commands you use a lot how to add color, a longer history, and a safety net against overwriting files 2.1 Where are executable programs installed? When you type ls, the shell runs a program called ls. That program is a file, sitting in a directory somewhere on your computer. So where is it, and how did the shell know where to look? 2.1.1 which and type which tells you where a command lives on the file system: which ls which less which python3 /bin/ls /usr/bin/less /usr/bin/python3 So ls is the file /bin/ls. You could run it by typing its full path, and it would do exactly the same thing: /bin/ls Now try which cd. In Zsh, you’ll get cd: shell built-in command. That’s because cd isn’t a program at all: it’s built into the shell itself (Section 1.3). type tells you what kind of command something is, whether it’s a builtin, a program, or an alias (Section 2.3): type cd type ls cd is a shell builtin ls is /bin/ls 2.1.2 The $PATH variable The shell finds programs using a variable called PATH, a list of directories separated by colons: echo $PATH /opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin Yours will look different. Colons are hard to read, so here’s a trick to print one directory per line. This is the PATH on the computer that built this book: echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' /usr/local/bin /System/Cryptexes/App/usr/bin /usr/bin /bin /usr/sbin /sbin /var/run/com.apple.security.cryptexd/codex.system/bootstrap/usr/local/bin /var/run/com.apple.security.cryptexd/codex.system/bootstrap/usr/bin /var/run/com.apple.security.cryptexd/codex.system/bootstrap/usr/appleinternal/bin /opt/X11/bin /Applications/quarto/bin /Library/TeX/texbin /usr/texbin /Applications/RStudio.app/Contents/Resources/app/quarto/bin /Applications/RStudio.app/Contents/Resources/app/bin/postback When you type a command, the shell: checks whether it’s an alias, a shortcut name you’ve defined for a longer command (Section 2.3), or a builtin, a command built into the shell itself, like cd (see type, above); if it’s neither, looks in each directory in your PATH, in order, for a program with that name; runs the first one it finds. If it doesn’t find the program in any of those directories, you get the dreaded message: zsh: command not found: blastn This means “I looked in every directory in your PATH, and no program has that name.” Either the program isn’t installed, or it is installed but in a directory that isn’t in your PATH. 2.1.3 Order matters You can have several programs with the same name in different directories. which -a lists all of them, in the order the shell searches: which -a python3 /usr/bin/python3 This computer has three different python3 programs: one from conda, one from Homebrew, and one from Apple. Typing python3 runs the first one, the conda version, because /opt/miniconda3/bin comes first in the PATH. This is the source of many “but it works on my computer!” mysteries. When a program behaves unexpectedly, which is one of the first things to check. Package managers edit your PATH. When you install conda or Homebrew, the installer adds lines to your shell’s configuration file (Section 2.2) that put its directories at the front of your PATH. That’s how conda’s python3 wins in the example above. 2.1.4 Why ./script.sh? This also explains why you have to type ./ to run your own script (Section 1.15). The current directory (.) isn’t in your PATH, so the shell won’t look there unless you give it the path to the script explicitly. (Leaving . out of the PATH is deliberate. It keeps a malicious program named, say, ls in some directory you cd into from running when you type ls.) 2.1.5 Changing the PATH PATH is a variable, so you can change it like any other variable (Section 1.12.1). To add a directory, include the current value, $PATH, plus the new directory, separated by a colon: export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/local/scripts" # add to the end: searched last export PATH="$HOME/local/scripts:$PATH" # add to the front: searched first export makes the variable available to programs that the shell runs, not just to the shell itself. PATH needs it. Adding to the end is the safer choice: your directory is searched last, so nothing in it can accidentally replace a standard command. Add to the front only when you specifically want your version of a program to win. Don’t forget the $PATH. What’s the difference between these two lines? export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/local/scripts" export PATH="$HOME/local/scripts" The first adds a directory to your PATH. The second replaces your entire PATH with a single directory, and suddenly nothing works: PATH=/nowhere ls echo "The shell can't find ls anymore." bash: line 1: ls: command not found The shell can't find ls anymore. If this happens, don’t panic. A change typed at the command line only lasts until you close the Terminal window, so just open a new one. If the bad line is in a configuration file, open a new window anyway and fix the file by calling the editor by its full path (for example, /usr/bin/nano ~/.zshrc). A PATH change typed at the command line lasts only for the current Terminal window. To make it permanent, put the export line in your shell’s configuration file, which runs every time you open a new window. That’s the subject of the rest of this chapter. 2.1.6 A home for your own scripts As you write more scripts, you’ll want to run them from anywhere, just like ls or grep, without typing ./ or a long path. The standard way to do that: Make a directory for your scripts, such as ~/local/scripts. Add that directory to your PATH, permanently. Put each script there, with a shebang line (Section 1.15) and execute permission (chmod u+x). Figure 2.1: Keep your own scripts in one directory, like ~/local/scripts, and add that directory to your PATH. Then you can run orf.py from any directory, just by typing its name. A common arrangement, borrowed from how Unix organizes its own files: Directory What goes there ~/local/scripts scripts you write yourself (Python, Bash, …) ~/local/src source code and downloaded software ~/local/bin executable programs you’ve installed or compiled yourself Add both ~/local/scripts and ~/local/bin to your PATH, and anything you put in them is always available. Exercise 2.1 Use which to find where grep, sort, nano, and python3 are installed. Use type on echo, pwd, and cd. Which are builtins? Print your PATH, one directory per line. How many directories does the shell search? Which is searched first? How many python3 programs are on your computer? Which one runs when you type python3? In a new Terminal window, run PATH=/nowhere, then try ls, pwd, and /bin/ls. Explain what works, what doesn’t, and why. Then close the window. 2.2 The shell’s configuration files Every time you open a Terminal window, the shell runs a configuration file (sometimes called a startup file or “dotfile”) from your home directory. Anything in that file, such as PATH changes, aliases, colors, and other settings, is applied before you see your first prompt. There’s virtually no limit to what you can set there. These files start with a ., so they’re hidden. Use ls -a to see them: ls -a ~ 2.2.1 Which file? It depends on your shell First, find out which shell you’re using: echo $SHELL On a Mac, it’s almost certainly /bin/zsh, the default since 2019. On Linux, including the computing cluster, it’s usually /bin/bash. Each shell reads different files: File Shell When it runs ~/.zshrc Zsh every interactive shell: every new Terminal window or tab ~/.zprofile Zsh login shells only, before .zshrc ~/.zshenv Zsh every Zsh, even ones that run scripts ~/.bash_profile Bash login shells: logging in with ssh, and every window in Mac Terminal ~/.bashrc Bash non-login interactive shells: new windows in most Linux terminals, or typing bash 2.2.2 Zsh: use ~/.zshrc If you use Zsh (most Mac users), put your settings in ~/.zshrc. It runs for every new Terminal window and tab, and it’s where you’ll find advice online telling you to put things. What about .zshenv? Some guides, and earlier versions of this course, put PATH changes in ~/.zshenv. That works too, but on macOS a system file that runs after .zshenv (/etc/zprofile) can reorder your PATH, moving your directories behind the system’s. Setting PATH in ~/.zshrc avoids that surprise. 2.2.3 Bash: .bash_profile vs. .bashrc Bash is more confusing, because it reads different files depending on whether the shell is a login shell: A login shell is the first shell you get when you log in: when you ssh into the cluster, for example. Bash runs ~/.bash_profile. A non-login shell is any other interactive shell: a new window in most Linux terminal programs, or a shell started by typing bash. Bash runs ~/.bashrc. To add to the confusion, the Mac Terminal app treats every new window as a login shell, so Bash on a Mac reads ~/.bash_profile. The usual solution is to put all your settings in ~/.bashrc, and have ~/.bash_profile read ~/.bashrc. Then your settings apply no matter how the shell starts. Make sure your ~/.bash_profile contains these lines (on most Linux systems, including the cluster, it already does): # in ~/.bash_profile: also read ~/.bashrc, if it exists if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then source ~/.bashrc fi 2.2.4 In short You’re using… Put your settings in… Zsh (the Mac default) ~/.zshrc Bash on the cluster or Linux ~/.bashrc (and check that ~/.bash_profile reads it) Bash on a Mac ~/.bash_profile, or ~/.bashrc read by ~/.bash_profile 2.2.5 Editing your configuration file Your configuration file is an ordinary text file, so edit it with nano or any text editor. Make a backup first: a mistake in this file can make every new Terminal window misbehave. cp ~/.zshrc ~/.zshrc.bak # back it up (skip this if the file doesn't exist yet) nano ~/.zshrc # edit it; nano creates it if it doesn't exist Changes take effect in new Terminal windows. To apply them to the window you’re in, source the file, which runs it in your current shell: source ~/.zshrc Lines starting with # are comments. To turn a setting off without deleting it, “comment it out” by putting a # at the start of the line. Don’t delete what you didn’t write. Conda, Homebrew, and other installers add blocks to your configuration file, often marked with comments like >>> conda initialize >>>. Leave those alone, and add your own settings above or below them. 2.3 Aliases An alias is a shortcut: a short name that the shell replaces with a longer command. Make one with alias name='command': alias cl='clear' alias cx='chmod u+x' alias ll='ls -lh' alias pin='ssh username@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu' Now typing cl clears the screen, cx myscript.sh makes a script executable, ll gives a long listing with human-readable sizes, and pin logs you onto the cluster. There are no spaces around the =, just like a variable. Put the command in single quotes, especially if it contains spaces. Anything you type after the alias is added to the end of the command, so cx myscript.sh becomes chmod u+x myscript.sh. An alias typed at the command line lasts until you close the window. Put it in your configuration file to keep it. alias # list all your aliases type ll # what does this alias stand for? unalias ll # remove an alias (for this session) A safety alias. Many people add alias rm='rm -i', so rm always asks before deleting. It’s a good idea while you’re learning. The catch: you can come to depend on it and then get burned on a computer that doesn’t have it. To skip an alias once, put a backslash in front of the command: \rm file. Aliases work only when you’re typing commands interactively; they don’t work inside scripts. For anything more complicated than a shortcut, write a script and put it in ~/local/scripts (Section 2.1.6). 2.4 Colors 2.4.1 Colors in ls output Color makes ls output much easier to scan: directories, executable programs, and links stand out from ordinary files. On a Mac, turn colors on and choose them with two variables in your configuration file: export CLICOLOR=1 export LSCOLORS=cxfxcxdxDxegedabagacad CLICOLOR=1 turns colors on. LSCOLORS chooses them. It’s a code of 11 pairs of letters; in each pair, the first letter is the text color and the second is the background color, for a different kind of file: Position Kind of file Above Meaning 1 directory cx green text, default background 2 symbolic link fx magenta 3 socket cx green 4 pipe dx brown 5 executable Dx bold brown (yellow) 6–11 special files you’ll rarely see egedabagacad various Letter Color Letter Color a black A bold black (gray) b red B bold red c green C bold green d brown D bold brown (yellow) e blue E bold blue f magenta F bold magenta g cyan G bold cyan h light gray H bold light gray (white) x default So to make directories bold blue instead of green, change the first pair from cx to Ex. Colors on Linux. The GNU ls on Linux uses a different system: colors are turned on with ls --color=auto (usually already set up as an alias) and chosen with a variable called LS_COLORS, in a different format. On the cluster, colors are probably on already. Older guides, including earlier versions of this course, also set export TERM=xterm-color. Modern versions of Terminal don’t need it, and it limits you to 8 colors, so leave it out. 2.4.2 Terminal colors, fonts, and themes The Terminal app itself has color themes. Open Terminal > Settings (Preferences on older versions of macOS), then the Profiles tab. Pick a theme from the list (Basic, Homebrew, Pro, Ocean, …), and click Default to use it for every new window. On the same tab, you can change the font and its size (stick with a monospace font) and the window size. 2.5 History The shell remembers the commands you’ve typed (Section 1.5). By default, it doesn’t remember many. Since your history is a record of what you did, it’s worth keeping a lot more of it, with dates. Zsh (in ~/.zshrc): HISTSIZE=50000 # commands to remember in the current session SAVEHIST=50000 # commands to save in the history file setopt EXTENDED_HISTORY # save the date and time of each command In Zsh, history shows only the last 16 commands. Use history 1 to see everything, and history -i 1 to include dates and times. Bash (in ~/.bashrc): HISTSIZE=50000 # commands to remember in the current session HISTFILESIZE=50000 # commands to save in the history file HISTTIMEFORMAT="%Y-%m-%d " # show the date of each command in `history` Combine your history with grep to find that command you ran last month: history 1 | grep blastn # Zsh history | grep blastn # Bash 2.6 A safety net: noclobber In Section 1.7, you saw that > overwrites an existing file without warning. Turn on the noclobber option, and the shell refuses to overwrite files with >: set -o noclobber set -o noclobber echo "oops" > fruit.txt echo "fruit.txt was not overwritten" bash: line 1: fruit.txt: cannot overwrite existing file fruit.txt was not overwritten When you really do mean to overwrite a file, use >| instead of >. noclobber works in both Bash and Zsh. Put it in your configuration file and it will save you from yourself at least once. 2.7 Customizing your prompt The prompt can show useful information, such as your user name, the computer you’re on (handy when you have windows open on several computers), and the directory you’re in. Set it with PROMPT in Zsh or PS1 in Bash. Each uses special codes: Shows Zsh (PROMPT) Bash (PS1) user name %n \u computer name %m \h current directory (full) %~ \w current directory (last part) %1~ \W %/# or $/# (# for administrators) %# \$ PROMPT='%n@%m %1~ %# ' # Zsh: aja@hostname nt % PS1='\u@\h \W \$ ' # Bash: aja@hostname nt $ 2.8 Putting it together Here’s a complete starting configuration file for Zsh on a Mac: # ~/.zshrc # PATH: my own scripts and programs export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/local/scripts:$HOME/local/bin" # colors for ls export CLICOLOR=1 export LSCOLORS=cxfxcxdxDxegedabagacad # history: remember a lot, with dates HISTSIZE=50000 SAVEHIST=50000 setopt EXTENDED_HISTORY # don't let > overwrite existing files (use >| to force it) set -o noclobber # aliases (keyboard shortcuts) alias cl='clear' alias cx='chmod u+x' alias ll='ls -lh' alias pin='ssh username@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu' And the equivalent for Bash on the cluster, in ~/.bashrc: # ~/.bashrc export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/local/scripts:$HOME/local/bin" HISTSIZE=50000 HISTFILESIZE=50000 HISTTIMEFORMAT="%Y-%m-%d " set -o noclobber alias cl='clear' alias cx='chmod u+x' alias ll='ls -lh' The course files include a sample configuration file, files/other_files/bash_profile.txt.
