Chapter 3 Organizing your project In this chapter how to lay out a project directory with data, scripts, results, figs, and manuscript folders how to document where your data came from in a data/README.md how to make an RStudio project how to keep a project notebook in R Markdown that records everything you did: the commands, the software versions, and the results how to write Markdown 3.1 Why organize? The most important collaborator on any project is you, six months from now. By then you’ll have forgotten which file is the raw data, which script made Figure 3, and what options you gave the aligner. A reviewer will ask, or a labmate will want to build on your work, or you’ll find a bug and need to redo everything downstream of it. Organizing a project well isn’t hard, and you only have to decide how once. The layout in this chapter follows two widely read papers that are worth a few minutes of your time: Noble (2009). A quick guide to organizing computational biology projects. PLoS Computational Biology 5: e1000424. Wilson et al. (2017). Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLoS Computational Biology 13: e1005510. The guiding principle, from Noble: someone unfamiliar with your project should be able to look at your files and understand exactly what you did and why. 3.2 A directory for each project Put each project in its own directory, with the same set of folders every time: Folder What goes in it data/ raw data, exactly as you received or downloaded it, plus a README.md saying where it came from scripts/ your code: shell scripts, Python, R results/ intermediate files made by your scripts: filtered and processed data, tables, alignments, trees, program output figs/ figures, made by your scripts manuscript/ the paper, poster, or thesis chapter Data flow in one direction: scripts read raw data from data/ and write what they make to results/; later scripts read from results/ and write more results, or figures in figs/. Nothing a script makes ever goes in data/. At the top level go a README.md describing the project and the project notebook (Section 3.5). Inside these folders, add subdirectories wherever they help you, or someone else, find things. Organize each folder by what’s in it. Our example project, on the genome of the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum, uses two kinds of data: the published genome sequence and our own RNA-seq reads: phaeodactylum_project/ ├── README.md ├── notebook.Rmd ├── phaeodactylum_project.Rproj ├── data/ │ ├── README.md │ ├── genome/ │ └── rnaseq/ ├── scripts/ │ └── seq_lengths.sh ├── results/ │ ├── 2026-01-16_seq_lengths/ │ ├── 2026-02-02_assembly_k21/ │ ├── 2026-02-03_assembly_k33/ │ └── 2026-02-05_assembly_k55/ ├── figs/ └── manuscript/ data/ is divided by source: one subdirectory for each data set, each described in data/README.md (Section 3.3). results/ is divided by analysis: each time you run an analysis, its output goes in a new subdirectory named with the date and what it is (Section 3.2.2). scripts/ and figs/ stay flat, with descriptive file names, until there are enough files that subdirectories would help. Why not a genome/ and rnaseq/ folder everywhere? You’ll sometimes see projects that repeat the same subdirectories inside data, scripts, results, and figs. That can work, but it’s rarely as clean as it looks: a script often uses data from more than one part of the project, a figure combines several results, and the parts of a project change as it goes. Start simple, and add subdirectories when a folder gets crowded. 3.2.1 Making the directories You could make these one at a time with mkdir, but the shell has a shortcut. Brace expansion turns a comma-separated list in braces into several words. See what it does with echo: echo {data,scripts,results,figs,manuscript} echo sample_{A,B,C}_{R1,R2}.fastq.gz data scripts results figs manuscript sample_A_R1.fastq.gz sample_A_R2.fastq.gz sample_B_R1.fastq.gz sample_B_R2.fastq.gz sample_C_R1.fastq.gz sample_C_R2.fastq.gz Two sets of braces give every combination. Braces can also go inside other braces, so one mkdir makes the whole tree. -p makes the parent directory, phaeodactylum_project, along the way (Section 1.9): mkdir -p phaeodactylum_project/{data/{genome,rnaseq},scripts,results,figs,manuscript} find phaeodactylum_project -type d | sort phaeodactylum_project phaeodactylum_project/data phaeodactylum_project/data/genome phaeodactylum_project/data/rnaseq phaeodactylum_project/figs phaeodactylum_project/manuscript phaeodactylum_project/results phaeodactylum_project/scripts No spaces inside the braces. {data, scripts} doesn’t expand, because the space splits it into two separate words. The same goes for spaces in file and directory names generally (Section 1.4). Prefer pictures? The tree command draws a directory tree like the one above. It isn’t installed by default: brew install tree on a Mac, sudo apt install tree on Linux. 3.2.2 Rules of thumb One project, one directory. Everything a project needs lives inside it, so you can move it, copy it to the cluster, or put it on GitHub as one unit. Raw data are read-only. Never edit raw data by hand. Scripts read the raw data and write their output to results/. To protect raw data from accidents, remove write permission (Section 1.15.3): chmod -R a-w data/genome. Everything in results/ and figs/ can be remade by running your scripts. If you deleted either folder, you should be able to get it back. That’s why the notebook records every command (Section 3.5). Results can be big, so they’re often left out of Git (Section 5.6) and backed up separately if they took a long time to make. Organize results by analysis. When you run the same analysis several ways, give each run its own subdirectory, such as results/2026-02-03_assembly_k33/, so new output never overwrites old output and the date links it to its notebook entry. Use relative paths inside the project, such as results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv, not /Users/aja/Desktop/phaeodactylum_project/results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv. Then the project works on any computer, in any location. Name files so they sort. Use dates in the form 2026-01-14 (year first), and number scripts that run in order: 01_download.sh, 02_seq_lengths.sh, 03_plot.R. Use leading zeros (01, not 1) so 10 sorts after 09. No spaces in names (Section 1.4). 3.2.3 Marking the final result Most analyses are run more than once: with a range of parameter settings, on different subsets of the data, or again after you fix a bug. That’s as it should be, but months later, when a reviewer asks about Figure 2, which of the dozen runs did you actually publish? Don’t copy the chosen output somewhere else, and don’t rename it. Leave every run where it is, and make a symbolic link (Section 1.9.4) called FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT that points to the exact file you used. Suppose we assembled a genome with three different k-mer sizes, and the paper uses the assembly made with k = 33: ls 2026-02-02_assembly_k21 2026-02-03_assembly_k33 2026-02-05_assembly_k55 Go to the directory where the link should live, and make the link: ln -s 2026-02-03_assembly_k33/contigs.fasta FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT ls -l total 0 drwxr-xr-x@ 3 aja staff 96 Nov 2 22:29 2026-02-02_assembly_k21 drwxr-xr-x@ 3 aja staff 96 Nov 2 22:29 2026-02-03_assembly_k33 drwxr-xr-x@ 3 aja staff 96 Nov 2 22:29 2026-02-05_assembly_k55 lrwxr-xr-x@ 1 aja staff 37 Nov 2 22:29 FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT -> 2026-02-03_assembly_k33/contigs.fasta ls -l shows where the link points (->), and the l at the start of the line marks it as a link. Anything that reads the link reads the real file: head -n 1 FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT >contig_1 k=33 Now the answer is obvious to you, your coauthors, and anyone who reuses your project, and the runs you didn’t use are still there for comparison. A few tips: Its name is in capitals so it stands out in a directory listing. Make one link per published result. If a paper uses several, give each link a descriptive suffix, such as FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT_fig2 and FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT_table1. The same works for figures: put a FINAL_PUBLISHED_FIG2 link in figs/. Changed your mind? ln -sf replaces an existing link: ln -sf 2026-02-05_assembly_k55/contigs.fasta FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT. Record the choice in your notebook, with the reason: “Used the k = 33 assembly: highest N50 and BUSCO completeness of the three.” A link’s target is relative to the link, not to you. ln -s stores the path to the target exactly as you typed it, and the system follows it from the directory where the link lives. If you’re at the top of the project and type ln -s results/2026-02-03_assembly_k33/contigs.fasta results/FINAL_PUBLISHED_RESULT, the link looks for results/2026-02-03_assembly_k33/... inside results/, and finds nothing: a broken link. That’s why it’s easiest to cd to the directory where the link should live first. Check a new link with head or ls -L, which show an error if the link is broken. Keep links relative. A link to a relative path, like the one above, keeps working when you move or copy the whole project, because the files it points to move with it. A link to an absolute path (/Users/aja/Desktop/phaeodactylum_project/...) breaks as soon as the project moves. rsync -a (Section 4.2.2) copies links as links, and Git stores them as links, too. 3.3 Documenting your data Every data directory gets its own README.md that says, for each data set: what it is, where it came from (a URL or accession number), when and how you got it, and its checksums (a kind of digital fingerprint for a file, covered in Section 4.5). This is the first thing you’ll need when you write the methods section, and the first thing anyone reusing your data will look for. Here’s how the genome data in our example project were downloaded. NCBI provides checksums for every file, so we check that the download is intact. Don’t worry about the details yet: downloading with curl and checking files with md5sum are covered in Chapter 4 (Sections 4.3 and 4.5). For now, notice what gets recorded: cd data/genome curl -O https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/150/955/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz curl -O https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/150/955/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2/md5checksums.txt md5sum GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz grep ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz md5checksums.txt 9f3ceb6ed3a6c00bd1019a44fdcf4256 GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz 9f3ceb6ed3a6c00bd1019a44fdcf4256 ./GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz Our checksum (first line) matches NCBI’s (second line). And here’s the data/README.md that records it all. It’s written in Markdown (Section 3.6): # Data for the Phaeodactylum genome project ## genome/ Reference genome of *Phaeodactylum tricornutum* CCAP 1055/1, RefSeq assembly GCF_000150955.2 (ASM15095v2), from NCBI: <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000150955.2/> Downloaded 2026-01-14 by Your Name. Commands are in `notebook.Rmd`. | File | Contents | MD5 | |---------------------------------------------|--------------------------|----------------------------------| | GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz | genome sequence (FASTA) | 9f3ceb6ed3a6c00bd1019a44fdcf4256 | | md5checksums.txt | NCBI's checksums | | ## rnaseq/ RNA-seq reads, 6 samples, sequenced by the UAMS Genomics Core, received 2026-02-03 on a hard drive. Sample information is in `rnaseq/samples.csv`. If one part of the project has a lot of data, it can have its own README, for example data/rnaseq/README.md, with data/README.md pointing to it. 3.4 RStudio projects RStudio is the most popular program for working in R, and it’s a good home base for a project even when most of the work happens in the shell. An RStudio project is a project directory with a small settings file, phaeodactylum_project.Rproj, at the top level. Opening a project (double-click the .Rproj file, or use File > Open Project in RStudio): sets R’s working directory to the top of the project, so relative paths such as results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv just work opens a Terminal tab (next to the Console) that also starts at the top of the project reopens the files you were working on, and keeps a separate history for each project To turn the directory we made into an RStudio project: In RStudio, choose File > New Project… Choose Existing Directory, browse to phaeodactylum_project, and click Create Project. RStudio restarts inside the project and creates phaeodactylum_project.Rproj and a hidden .Rproj.user/ directory of settings. (To start a project from scratch instead, choose New Directory > New Project, then make the folders from the Terminal tab.) The .Rproj file is short plain text: Version: 1.0 RestoreWorkspace: No SaveWorkspace: No AlwaysSaveHistory: Default EnableCodeIndexing: Yes Encoding: UTF-8 Start each R session fresh. In Tools > Global Options > General, uncheck Restore .RData into workspace at startup and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never. Otherwise R quietly carries old objects from one session to the next, and code that works for you may fail for everyone else. If everything important is made by scripts, you never need a saved workspace. 3.5 The project notebook At the bench, you keep a lab notebook. A computational project needs one too. The project notebook is where you document everything you do, as you do it: what you did and why, dated the exact commands you ran, copied from the Terminal the versions of the software you used (results can change between versions, and the methods section needs them) the results, including the dead ends (“tried X; it didn’t work because Y”) what to do next We’ll keep the notebook in R Markdown, a plain-text format that mixes Markdown text (Section 3.6) with chunks of code. Knitting the file turns it into a nicely formatted web page, with the code in shaded boxes. (This book was written in R Markdown, too.) 3.5.1 Making the notebook In RStudio, with the project open: Choose File > New File > R Markdown… Give it a title, such as “Phaeodactylum genome project: notebook”, and your name. Leave the output format as HTML. Click OK. RStudio opens an example document. Delete everything below the header (the part between the two --- lines), and save the file as notebook.Rmd at the top of the project. Click Knit (or press Cmd+Shift+K) to turn notebook.Rmd into notebook.html, and open it in a browser. R Markdown or Quarto? RStudio’s File > New File menu also offers Quarto documents (.qmd), the newer successor to R Markdown from the same developers. They work almost the same way. This course uses R Markdown, which is still fully supported. 3.5.2 What goes in the notebook Here’s a notebook for our example project, a couple of days in. Entries are in date order, each under a dated heading, with the commands in code chunks and the results written out below them: --- title: "Phaeodactylum genome project: notebook" author: "Your Name" date: "Started 2026-01-14. Last knitted `r Sys.Date()`." output: html_document: toc: true toc_float: true --- ```{r setup, include = FALSE} # This notebook is a record of what I did. Knitting it shouldn't rerun # downloads or long analyses, so chunks don't run unless I say eval = TRUE. knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE) ``` # About this project **Question:** How are genes distributed across the chromosomes of the diatom *Phaeodactylum tricornutum*? **Layout:** raw data in `data/` (sources in `data/README.md`), code in `scripts/`, intermediate files in `results/` (one dated subdirectory per analysis), figures in `figs/`, writing in `manuscript/`. # Software | Program | Version | Installed with | |---------|---------|---------------------| | curl | 8.7.1 | comes with macOS | | R | 4.5.2 | cran.r-project.org | # 2026-01-14: Download the reference genome Downloaded the genome sequence (RefSeq assembly GCF_000150955.2) from NCBI and checked it against NCBI's checksums. Details in `data/README.md`. ```{bash} cd data/genome curl -O https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/150/955/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz curl -O https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/150/955/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2/md5checksums.txt md5sum GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz grep ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz md5checksums.txt ``` **Result:** checksums match (`9f3ceb6ed3a6c00bd1019a44fdcf4256`). # 2026-01-16: Sequence lengths How many sequences are in the assembly, and how long are they? ```{bash} gzcat data/genome/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz | grep -c '>' gzcat data/genome/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz | grep -c chromosome mkdir results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths bash scripts/seq_lengths.sh > results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv ``` **Result:** 88 sequences, 33 of them chromosomes. The longest is chromosome 1 (NC_011669.1, 2,535,400 bp). ```{r} lengths <- read.table("results/2026-01-16_seq_lengths/seq_lengths.tsv", col.names = c("id", "bp")) png("figs/seq_lengths.png") hist(log10(lengths$bp), main = "", xlab = "Sequence length (log10 bp)") dev.off() ``` ![Lengths of the 88 sequences in the assembly.](figs/seq_lengths.png) **Next:** download the annotation (GFF) and count genes per chromosome. # R session ```{r session-info, eval = TRUE} sessionInfo() ``` A few things to notice: The header (between the --- lines) is written in YAML. It sets the title, author, and date, and toc: true adds a table of contents that floats beside the text (toc_float), so you can jump to any day. Code chunks start with ```{bash} or ```{r} and end with ```. RStudio shows them shaded, and the Insert menu (the green +C button above the editor) adds a new one. eval = FALSE in the setup chunk means knitting doesn’t run the code. The notebook is a record: you ran the commands in the Terminal as you worked, and you don’t want every knit to download the genome again. Turn a chunk back on with eval = TRUE in its header, as in the last chunk. Software versions are in a table, copied from each program’s version command (curl --version, samtools --version, blastn -version). The last chunk runs sessionInfo(), which lists the versions of R and of every R package that was loaded. Longer code goes in scripts/. The notebook just records running it. Here’s scripts/seq_lengths.sh, which uses awk (Section 1.13) to print the name and length of each sequence in a FASTA file: #!/bin/bash # Print the name and length of every sequence in the genome, tab-separated. gzcat data/genome/GCF_000150955.2_ASM15095v2_genomic.fna.gz | awk '/^>/ {if (name) print name "\t" len; name = substr($1, 2); len = 0; next} {len += length($0)} END {print name "\t" len}' Write it down now. The commands you think you’ll remember are the ones you’ll forget. Paste each command into the notebook right after it works (or right after it fails, with a note about why). history (Section 2.5) can help you recover what you typed. 3.6 Markdown Markdown is a simple way to format plain text. You write **bold**, and it becomes bold. It’s everywhere in scientific computing: R Markdown and Quarto documents, Jupyter notebooks, README.md files, and GitHub, which displays Markdown files formatted. Because it’s plain text, Markdown is easy to read even before it’s formatted, works with any text editor, and works well with Git (Chapter 5), which we’ll use to keep track of every version of your project. Text You type You get *italic* or _italic_ italic **bold** bold `code` code ~~strikethrough~~ strikethrough H~2~O, x^2^ (R Markdown) H2O, x2 [a link](https://www.uark.edu) a link <https://www.uark.edu> https://www.uark.edu Use italics for species names: *Phaeodactylum tricornutum*. Paragraphs are separated by a blank line. A single line break inside a paragraph is ignored, so you can break long lines wherever you like. To start a new paragraph, leave a blank line. Headings Start a line with one to six # characters, followed by a space: # Heading 1 ## Heading 2 ### Heading 3 Lists Start each item with - (or *) for a bulleted list, or a number and a period for a numbered list. Indent by four spaces to nest a list inside another. Leave a blank line before a list. Things to buy: - agarose - primers - ITS1 - ITS4 Steps: 1. Extract DNA. 2. Amplify. 3. Sequence. Code Inline code goes between single backticks, `like this`. For a block of code, put three backticks on the lines before and after. Add the language after the opening backticks to color-code it: ```bash grep -c '>' sequences.fasta ``` In R Markdown, a language in braces, such as ```{bash} or ```{r}, makes a code chunk that can be run, not just displayed. Images, tables, and quotes ![A caption for the figure](figs/seq_lengths.png) | Sample | Reads | |--------|-----------| | A1 | 1,204,551 | | A2 | 998,013 | > A block quote starts with a greater-than sign. An image is a link with a ! in front; the text in brackets becomes the caption. In a table, the | characters don’t need to line up, but it’s easier to read when they do. RStudio’s Visual editor (the button at the top left of the editor) lets you edit Markdown as formatted text and insert tables, images, and links from menus, and switch back to Source to see the Markdown. Literal characters. To show a character that Markdown would otherwise interpret, like * or #, put a backslash in front: \*not italic\*. Chapter 4 Working remotely In this chapter how to log onto a remote computer, such as the university’s computing cluster, with ssh how to copy files between computers with scp and rsync how to download data from the web with curl and wget how to compress and archive files with gzip and tar how to check that data arrived intact with checksums (md5sum) how to write a job script and submit it to the SLURM job scheduler how to set up SSH keys so you don’t have to type your password every time Sooner or later, your data will be too big or your analyses too slow for your laptop. Then it’s time to use a high-performance computing (HPC) cluster: a large collection of computers that many people share. At the University of Arkansas, that’s the Arkansas High Performance Computing Center (AHPCC). Working on a cluster involves a few related tasks, which this chapter covers in order: logging on, copying files, retrieving data, compressing data, verifying data, preparing job scripts, and submitting jobs. Figure 4.1: How the pieces fit together. You log onto the cluster’s login node from your own computer. From there, you submit jobs to the SLURM scheduler, which runs them on the compute nodes. The login node and compute nodes share the same storage, so your files are available everywhere. 4.1 Logging onto a remote system ssh establishes a secure shell on a remote computer. Once you’re logged in, you type commands exactly as you would in your own Terminal, but they run on the remote machine. ssh requires you to authenticate, usually with a password (or with keys, Section 4.7). It’s secure: your login and everything else you send are encrypted as they travel across the network. Older, insecure ways of connecting (telnet, rlogin, and ftp) send everything, including your password, as plain text. Don’t use them. OpenSSH, the standard ssh program, comes with macOS and Linux, and with Windows 10 and 11 (run it in PowerShell or Windows Terminal). To log onto the AHPCC cluster: ssh username@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu Replace username with your UARK username, and use your UARK password. A few things to know the first time: ssh will ask whether you trust the remote computer (“The authenticity of host … can’t be established”). Type yes. It won’t ask again. When you type your password, nothing appears on the screen, not even dots. That’s normal. Type it and press Return. Your prompt changes to show that you’re on the remote computer. Use exit to log off and return to your own computer. The cluster runs Linux, and your shell there is Bash, not Zsh. Your aliases and other settings from your Mac don’t come with you; to customize your shell on the cluster, edit ~/.bashrc there (Section 2.2). Adopt a single username. If your username on your own computer is the same as on the remote computer, you can leave it out: ssh hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu # instead of... ssh username@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu Save time by using the same username for all your accounts. 4.1.1 The file system on AHPCC Location What it’s for /home/username where you are when you log in (on the login node) /storage/username where to store your data $HOME or /storage where to run standard jobs from /scratch/$SLURM_JOB_ID where to run jobs that do lots of reading and writing (Section 4.6.2) /share/apps where programs are installed Don’t run analyses on the login node. The login node is shared by everyone who is logged in. It’s for editing files, moving data, and submitting jobs. Anything that takes more than a minute or so, or uses lots of memory, belongs in a job on the compute nodes (Section 4.6). Heavy work on the login node slows it down for everyone. Exercise 4.1 Log onto hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu. Where are you? Use pwd and ls -la to look around your home directory. Find your storage directory and check how much space you’re using there with du -sh. Use ls /share/apps to see what programs are installed. Log off. 4.2 Copying files between computers 4.2.1 scp scp (secure copy) copies files between computers. It uses ssh to transfer the data, so it offers the same security as ssh, and asks for the same password. It works just like cp: source first, destination second. scp [options] source destination The difference is that either the source or the destination (or both) can be on another computer. A remote location looks like this: username@host:path/to/filename └──┬───┘ └┬─┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ └── path on the remote computer (relative to your home directory there, │ │ unless it starts with /); leave it out to mean your home directory │ └── the remote computer, followed by a colon (:) └── your username on the remote computer, followed by @ (optional if it's the same) The colon is what tells scp that a location is on another computer. Forget it, and scp just makes a local copy with a strange name. Copying to a remote computer: # copy a file to your remote home directory, giving it a new name scp nad4.fasta aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:new_file.fasta # copy a file to your remote home directory, keeping its name scp nad4.fasta aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu: To copy a directory, add -r, just like cp -r: # keep the same directory name, in your remote home directory scp -r nt aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu: # copy into an existing remote directory, with a new name scp -r nt aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:test_dir/copied_nt # copy into your storage directory (an absolute path), keeping the same name scp -r nt aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:/storage/aja Copying from a remote computer just swaps the order. Run these on your computer, not on the cluster: # copy from your remote home directory into the current directory, with a new name scp aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:nad4.fasta nad4_copied.fasta # copy from a remote directory into the current directory (.), keeping the same name scp aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:blast_output/nad4.blastn . # copy into a local directory, keeping the same name scp aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:nad4.fasta biol5153/watermelon_genome/ # copy a whole directory from the remote computer scp -r hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:blast_output biol5153/watermelon_genome/ Where do I run scp? Almost always on your own computer. Your laptop knows how to find the cluster (hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu), but the cluster has no way to find your laptop. Exercise 4.2 Copy watermelon_genome/nt/nad4.fasta to your home directory on the cluster. Log on and check that it’s there. On the cluster, make a directory called biol5153. Back on your own computer, copy the whole watermelon_genome/nt directory into it. On the cluster, rename nad4.fasta to nad4_remote.fasta. Then copy it back to your own computer’s Desktop. 4.2.2 rsync: bigger, smarter copies rsync synchronizes files and directories, locally or between computers. For anything big, it’s better than scp: It only sends the differences between versions. If a transfer gets interrupted, or you change a few files, running the same rsync command again sends only what’s missing or changed. It can compress data while sending it. Its archive option preserves links, timestamps, permissions, ownership, and other attributes. rsync [options] source destination Option Effect -a, --archive archive mode: recursive, and preserve links, timestamps, etc. -r, --recursive recurse into directories (included in -a) -l, --links preserve symbolic links (included in -a) -v, --verbose print lots of information about what it’s doing -z, --compress compress data as it’s sent -n, --dry-run show what would be copied, without copying anything In practice, rsync -av (local) and rsync -azv (between computers) are all you’ll usually need. # synchronize a local directory to the cluster rsync -azv my_data aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu: # ...into a new destination directory name rsync -azv my_data aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:my_data_new_name # synchronize from the cluster to your computer rsync -azv aja@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu:blast_output . rsync: mind the / rsync is picky about a trailing slash on the source: No trailing slash (mt_genomes) copies the directory itself, including everything in it. Trailing slash (mt_genomes/) copies only the contents of the directory, not the directory itself. Here’s the difference, copying into two empty directories: mkdir -p copy1 copy2 rsync -a nt copy1 # no slash: copies the directory rsync -a nt/ copy2 # slash: copies what's inside it ls copy1 | head -n 3 echo --- ls copy2 | head -n 3 nt --- atp1.fasta atp4.fasta atp6.fasta Use -n first. rsync -avn lists exactly what would be copied, without copying anything. When the list looks right, run it again without the n. Moving files with a graphical program If you prefer drag and drop, programs such as FileZilla and Cyberduck provide a graphical front end for copying files over SSH. Choose the SFTP protocol when you connect. 4.3 Getting data from the web Most public data (genomes, sequencing reads, protein structures) is distributed through websites and FTP servers. Clicking “Download” works for one file on your laptop, but not for 200 files, or on a cluster with no web browser. Use curl or wget instead. 4.3.1 curl curl (“see URL”) downloads files without any interaction. It’s installed on macOS, Linux, and Windows. Option Effect -o name write the output to a file named name -O write the output to a file with the same name as on the server -L follow redirects (if the file has moved, go to its new location) -C - continue (resume) an interrupted download By default, curl writes the file to STDOUT, so you’ll almost always want -o or -O: # download green fluorescent protein's structure from the Protein Data Bank, # printing it to the screen (not very useful) curl https://files.rcsb.org/download/1EMA.pdb # write it to a file of your choosing curl -o gfp.pdb https://files.rcsb.org/download/1EMA.pdb # write it to a file with the same name as on the server (1EMA.pdb) curl -O https://files.rcsb.org/download/1EMA.pdb # download several files at once (the braces work in curl itself; keep the quotes) curl -O "https://files.rcsb.org/download/{1EMA,1GFL,1G7K}.pdb" Use -L when files have moved. Websites reorganize. When a file has moved, the server sends back a “redirect” pointing to the new location, and curl stops there unless you add -L. You’ll end up with an empty or tiny file instead of your data. If a download is suspiciously small, check it with less, and add -L. 4.3.2 wget wget is another tool for downloading files, especially good at downloading many files from a site at once. It’s installed on most Linux systems, including the cluster. It isn’t installed on macOS by default; you can get it with Homebrew (brew install wget). Unlike curl, wget saves files with their original names by default. Option Effect -A, --accept only download files matching this pattern -R, --reject don’t download files matching this pattern -r, --recursive download recursively (warning: very aggressive) --no-parent don’t climb up into parent directories when recursing -c, --continue resume an interrupted download --user=username username for password-protected sites --ask-password prompt for the password # download human chromosome 22 from the UCSC Genome Browser wget https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg19/chromosomes/chr22.fa.gz # download all the GFF files from a colleague's server wget --accept "*.gff" --level 2 -r --no-directories --no-parent \ ftp://server.university.edu/labsite/annotations/ # download from a password-protected FTP site (a sequencing center, for example) wget --recursive --user=username --ask-password ftp://192.169.8.66/CleanData (A \ at the very end of a line continues the command on the next line.) Keep passwords out of your commands. You may see instructions that put a password right in the URL (ftp://username:password@server/...). It works, but the password is saved in your shell history, where anyone with access to your account can read it. Use --ask-password instead. Exercise 4.3 Use curl to download the structure of green fluorescent protein (PDB ID 1EMA) and save it as gfp.pdb. The atomic coordinates are on lines that start with ATOM. How many atoms are in the structure? Column 4 of the ATOM lines is the amino acid. How many different amino acids are there? (Hint: awk '$1 == "ATOM" { print $4 }', then sort and uniq.) Try curl -O http://www.rcsb.org/pdb/files/1ema.pdb, an old address for the same file. What did you get? Fix it. 4.4 Compressing data Compress big files before moving them. Sequence data compress well, often to a quarter of their original size, which means faster transfers and less storage. 4.4.1 gzip and gunzip gzip compresses files, and gunzip decompresses them. Compressed files end in .gz. By default, gzip and gunzip work in place: gzip file replaces file with file.gz, and gunzip file.gz replaces file.gz with file. No new copy is created. gzip can also compress STDIN, writing the result to STDOUT, so it works at the end of a pipe. Option Effect -c write to STDOUT and leave the original alone (useful for making copies) -d decompress (the same as gunzip) -k keep the original file instead of replacing it ls -lh watermelon.fsa gzip watermelon.fsa # compress (watermelon.fsa is replaced) ls -lh watermelon.fsa* -rw-------@ 1 aja staff 371K Nov 2 22:29 watermelon.fsa -rw-------@ 1 aja staff 108K Nov 2 22:29 watermelon.fsa.gz gunzip watermelon.fsa.gz # decompress (watermelon.fsa.gz is replaced) ls -lh watermelon.fsa* -rw-------@ 1 aja staff 371K Nov 2 22:29 watermelon.fsa gzip -c watermelon.fsa > wat.fsa.gz # make a compressed copy; keep the original gzip -d wat.fsa.gz # decompress, same as gunzip my_program.py reads.fa | gzip > out.fa.gz # compress a program's output on the fly 4.4.2 Working with compressed files You often don’t need to decompress a file to work with it: Command Like Does zcat cat print a compressed file zless less page through a compressed file zgrep grep search a compressed file gzip -k watermelon.fsa zgrep -o GAATTC watermelon.fsa.gz | wc -l # how many EcoRI sites in the genome? 168 On a Mac, use gzcat, not zcat. For historical reasons, macOS’s zcat only works on an old compression format (.Z files) and fails on .gz files with a confusing error. Use gzcat on a Mac, and zcat on Linux and the cluster. gunzip -c works everywhere. gzcat watermelon.fsa.gz | head -n 2 | cut -c 1-60 # zcat on Linux >watermelon [organism=Citrullus lanatus] [common=watermelon] ACGACAAATCCGGTCCGATGGCTGTTCTCCACTAACCACAAGGATATAGGGACTCTATAT 4.4.3 tar: archiving directories gzip compresses single files. To bundle a whole directory into one file, use tar (originally for tape archives). tar preserves the directory structure, and with -z it compresses the archive with gzip. The result is a “tarball,” ending in .tar.gz or .tgz, like the files.tgz you downloaded for this course. Option Effect -c create an archive -x extract an archive -t list the contents of an archive -z compress or decompress with gzip -v verbose: list each file as it’s processed -f name the archive file to create or read The trickiest part is that -f must be followed by the name of the archive. Put it last in the group of options, and you’ll get it right: -czf, -xzf, -tzf. To remember the first letter: create, extract, list. tar -czf genomes.tgz mt_genomes/ # create a compressed archive of mt_genomes ls -lh genomes.tgz du -sh mt_genomes -rw-r--r--@ 1 aja staff 3.3M Nov 2 22:29 genomes.tgz 11M mt_genomes tar -tzf genomes.tgz | head -n 4 # list what's inside, without extracting mt_genomes/ mt_genomes/nicotiana_tabacum.fasta mt_genomes/cycas_taitungensis.fasta mt_genomes/zea_mays_parviglumis.fasta tar -xzf genomes.tgz # extract everything tar -xzvf genomes.tgz # ...and list each file as it's extracted To extract a single file, give its path exactly as it appears in the archive (use tar -tzf to check): mkdir -p extracted && cd extracted tar -xzf ../genomes.tgz mt_genomes/ricinus.fasta find . . ./mt_genomes ./mt_genomes/ricinus.fasta tar -c overwrites. Like >, creating an archive overwrites any existing file with the same name, without asking. And watch the order of the arguments: tar -czf mt_genomes/ genomes.tgz is wrong, and will try to create an archive named mt_genomes/. Exercise 4.4 Compress a copy of watermelon.gbf with gzip -k. How much smaller is the compressed file? Without decompressing it, count the lines in the compressed file. Make a single file of all the sequences in watermelon_genome/nt, compress it, and copy it to a new directory, $HOME/mt_seqs, on the cluster. Archive and compress the whole watermelon_genome/aa directory into aa.tgz. List its contents. Then, in a new empty directory, extract only cox1.fasta from it. Copy aa.tgz to the cluster, log on, and extract it there. 4.5 Verifying data integrity Downloads of large files (raw sequence data, for example) can take hours, and network connections can drop out partway through, leaving you with partial or corrupted data that may look perfectly normal. You need a way to verify that your copy is identical to the original. The solution is a checksum: a short “fingerprint” calculated from every byte of a file. Checksum algorithms are deterministic: the same data always give the same checksum. Changing even a single byte gives a completely different checksum. Checksums are written in hexadecimal (the digits 0–9 and letters a–f). MD5 checksums are 32 characters long. SHA-1 checksums are 40 characters, and SHA-256 checksums are 64. MD5 is the most common for checking data transfers; SHA-256 is preferred when security matters. The process: Whoever provides the data calculates checksums for the original files and stores them in a text file. You download the data and the checksum file. You calculate checksums for your downloaded copies. You compare the two sets of values. Any difference means a file is corrupted, so download it again. 4.5.1 md5sum md5sum calculates MD5 checksums. Each line of output has the checksum, then the file name: md5sum cowboy_carter.txt 18fbb44d29fe657a1ce63b5f78b2675c cowboy_carter.txt The course files include cowboy_carter.md5sum, a checksum file of the kind that a sequencing center would give you: cat cowboy_carter.md5sum 18fbb44d29fe657a1ce63b5f78b2675c cowboy_carter.txt The checksums match, so the file is intact. Rather than comparing long strings by eye, let md5sum -c (check) do it. It reads the checksum file, recalculates each file’s checksum, and reports OK or FAILED: md5sum -c cowboy_carter.md5sum cowboy_carter.txt: OK You can also save your own checksums and compare the two files with diff (Section 1.10.7). No output means they’re identical: md5sum cowboy_carter.txt > my_checksums.md5sum diff my_checksums.md5sum cowboy_carter.md5sum Here’s what happens when a file changes by a single character: sed -i.bak 's/PROTECTOR/PROTECTER/' cowboy_carter.txt md5sum -c cowboy_carter.md5sum md5sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match cowboy_carter.txt: FAILED Checksums on a Mac. Recent versions of macOS include md5sum. On older versions, use md5 -r, which prints the same format. For SHA checksums, use shasum -a 256 file on a Mac and sha256sum file on Linux. Both accept -c. Exercise 4.5 Calculate the MD5 checksum of watermelon.fsa. Compress it with gzip -k and calculate the checksum of watermelon.fsa.gz. Are they the same? Why not? Calculate MD5 checksums for every file in watermelon_genome/nt and save them to nt.md5sum (one command). Copy nt and nt.md5sum to the cluster with scp -r. On the cluster, use md5sum -c to verify that every file arrived intact. Make a copy of nt on your own computer, change one letter in one of the files, and show that md5sum -c catches it. 4.6 Running jobs on the cluster To run an analysis on the cluster, you don’t run it directly. You describe it in a job script and submit the script to a job scheduler, which puts it in a queue and runs it on the compute nodes when the resources you asked for become available. There are different scheduling systems. Older clusters often use TORQUE/PBS; AHPCC uses SLURM. The ideas are the same in all of them. The process: Get all your data in place on the cluster (Section 4.1.1). Write a job script that includes: all the information the scheduler needs to run your job (how many processors, for how long, and so on); all the commands you want to run, exactly as you would type them on the command line. Submit your job script to the queue. 4.6.1 Anatomy of a SLURM script A SLURM job script is a Bash script (Section 1.15) with some extra lines at the top. Lines starting with #SBATCH are instructions for the scheduler. Bash treats them as comments, but SLURM reads them. #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=atp9.blast #SBATCH --partition comp72 #SBATCH --qos comp #SBATCH --nodes=1 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32 #SBATCH --time=72:00:00 #SBATCH -o %j.out #SBATCH -e %j.err #SBATCH --mail-type=ALL #SBATCH --mail-user=username@uark.edu cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR # job commands here command1 command2 Line What it does #!/bin/bash the shebang: this is a Bash script --job-name=atp9.blast a name for your job, so you can recognize it in the queue --partition comp72 which queue (partition) to run in --qos comp the quality of service, which goes with the partition --nodes=1 how many compute nodes --cpus-per-task=32 how many processor cores. Take only what you need. --time=72:00:00 the maximum wall time (hours:minutes:seconds); the job is killed after this -o %j.out, -e %j.err files for STDOUT and STDERR; any names you want (%j is the job ID number) --mail-type=ALL email you when the job starts, ends, or fails --mail-user=... where to send the email cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR move into the directory you submitted the job from command1, … the commands to run files/other_files/slurm-template.slurm in the course files is a template to start from. Ask what partitions are available with sinfo (below), and check the AHPCC documentation for which to use. Why cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR? SLURM sets the variable $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR to the directory you ran sbatch from. SLURM starts jobs in that directory anyway, but other schedulers (like PBS) start them in your home directory, and your script may cd somewhere else along the way. This line makes it explicit where the job runs, so the script behaves the same everywhere. 4.6.2 Using the scratch disk For jobs that read and write lots of data, run them on the fast scratch disk of the compute node, then copy the results back. SLURM creates a directory for each job at /scratch/$SLURM_JOB_ID. Put something like this in the commands part of your script: # copy input files to the scratch disk rsync -arl * /scratch/$SLURM_JOB_ID/ # cd into the scratch folder to run the job cd /scratch/$SLURM_JOB_ID # run the job command1 command2 # copy the output files back to the original folder when the job has finished rsync -arl /scratch/$SLURM_JOB_ID/* $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/ 4.6.3 Submitting and checking jobs Command What it does sinfo -l list the partitions (queues) on the cluster sbatch job_script.slurm submit a job; prints the job ID squeue -l -u username check the status of your jobs squeue --start -j jobID when will my job start? scancel jobID cancel (kill) a job scancel -u username cancel all your jobs scancel -t PENDING -u username cancel all your jobs that haven’t started 4.6.4 Software modules The cluster has hundreds of programs installed, many in several versions. To keep them from conflicting, they’re packaged as modules that you load when you need them, either at the command line or in your job script: module avail # what modules are available? module avail blast # ...matching "blast" module load blast # load a module module list # what modules do I have loaded? module purge # unload all modules Exercise 4.6 Log onto the cluster and use sinfo to see what partitions are available. Use module avail blast to find the BLAST module. Copy files/other_files/slurm-template.slurm and the files/data folder to the cluster. Edit the template with nano so that it runs in the data directory and prints letters.txt to STDOUT. Submit it with sbatch, and check on it with squeue. When the job finishes, look at its .out and .err files. What’s in each? Write a SLURM script that BLASTs the watermelon atp9 gene (nt/atp9.fasta) against the watermelon genome (watermelon.fsa). You’ll need makeblastdb -in watermelon.fsa -dbtype nucl to build a BLAST database first, then blastn -query nt/atp9.fasta -db watermelon.fsa. Write the output to atp9.vs.watermelon.blastn. Modify your script from question 4 so that it runs on the scratch disk. Submit a job, then cancel it with scancel before it finishes. 4.7 Authentication with SSH keys Typing your password every time you use ssh, scp, or rsync gets old. SSH keys are a safe and easy alternative: you create a matched pair of keys on your computer, a private key that never leaves your computer and a public key that you put on any computer you want to log onto. When you connect, ssh uses the pair to prove that you are who you say you are, without sending a password. You’ll also need SSH keys (or something similar) to push your work to GitHub, later in the course. Do this on your own. Setting up keys is straightforward, but every computer is a little different. Work through it outside of class, and ask if you get stuck. 1. Check for existing keys On your own computer, look in the hidden .ssh directory in your home directory: ls -la ~/.ssh If you see a pair of files like id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub (or id_rsa and id_rsa.pub), you already have keys. Skip to step 3. 2. Create a key pair ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -t ed25519 sets the type of key. Ed25519 is the current recommended type: it’s short, fast, and secure. (Older instructions use ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 2048. RSA keys still work, but if you make one, use at least -b 4096 bits.) When asked where to save the key, press Return to accept the default. When asked for a passphrase, you can press Return for no passphrase, or enter one for extra security (step 5 shows how to avoid typing it every time). This creates two files in ~/.ssh: File What it is id_ed25519 your private key. Never share it, copy it to another computer, or email it. id_ed25519.pub your public key. Safe to share; this is what goes on remote computers. 3. Copy your public key to the remote computer The easiest way is ssh-copy-id, which comes with macOS and Linux: ssh-copy-id username@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu Enter your password one last time. ssh-copy-id appends your public key to the file ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the remote computer and sets its permissions correctly. If ssh-copy-id isn’t available, do the same thing by hand: On your computer, print your public key and copy the whole line: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Log onto the remote computer: ssh username@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu Make sure the .ssh directory exists: mkdir -p ~/.ssh Paste your public key onto the end of authorized_keys, as one line: nano ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Set the permissions (step 4, below), then exit. 4. Check permissions ssh refuses to use keys if other people could change them. If you’re still asked for a password, set the permissions on the remote computer so that only you can read and write these files: chmod 700 ~/.ssh # only you can enter the directory chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys # only you can read or write the file These use the numeric form of chmod: 7 means read + write + execute, 6 means read + write, and 0 means nothing, for the user, group, and others, in that order. (On your own computer, the private key should also be 600.) 5. Log on ssh username@hpc-portal2.hpc.uark.edu You should be logged in without a password. If you set a passphrase on your key, you’ll be asked for it instead. To avoid typing the passphrase every time, add the key to the SSH agent, which remembers it for you: eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" # start the SSH agent ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # Mac: remember the passphrase in your Keychain ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # Linux Exercise 4.7 Set up SSH keys for the cluster, and log on without a password. Copy a file to the cluster with scp. Were you asked for a password? 4.8 Command summary Command What it does ssh user@host log onto a remote computer scp source user@host:dest copy a file to a remote computer (-r for directories) scp user@host:source dest copy a file from a remote computer rsync -av source dest synchronize files and directories (-z to compress, -n for a dry run) curl -O url download a file, keeping its name (-L to follow redirects) curl -o name url download a file to a name of your choosing wget url download a file gzip, gunzip compress, decompress (-k to keep the original) zcat/gzcat, zless, zgrep print, page through, or search a compressed file tar -czf archive.tgz dir/ create a compressed archive of a directory tar -tzf archive.tgz list the contents of an archive tar -xzf archive.tgz extract an archive md5sum file calculate a checksum md5sum -c checksums.md5sum verify files against a list of checksums sinfo list the cluster’s partitions (queues) sbatch script.slurm submit a job squeue -u user check on your jobs scancel jobID cancel a job module avail, module load find and load installed software ssh-keygen, ssh-copy-id create SSH keys; install your public key on a remote computer

Chapter 5 Version control with Git and GitHub In this chapter why scientists should use version control how to install and configure Git the Git workflow: track, stage, and commit how to undo changes, ignore files, and see what changed and when how to retrieve an old version of a file how to experiment safely with branches, and how to resolve a merge conflict how to back up and share your work on GitHub A note about GitHub. Git and GitHub aren’t the same thing. Git is free, open-source software that runs on your own computer. GitHub is a company that hosts Git repositories online, and Microsoft has owned it since 2018. Some people have started moving their projects off GitHub. Concerns include Microsoft’s ownership and the use of code hosted on GitHub to train Microsoft’s AI models, including the Copilot coding assistant, without the permission of the people who wrote the code. Some are moving to alternatives such as Forgejo, a community-run platform that you can host yourself or use through services such as Codeberg. Things are changing quickly, and it’s not yet clear where the field will settle. For now, though, GitHub is still the most established and widely used platform, and it’s the one this chapter uses. Everything you learn about Git itself works the same way on any of them. 5.1 Why version control? Every project changes over time. At the bench, you keep a lab notebook so you always have a before-and-after record: the PCR stopped working, so you changed the annealing temperature; a cheaper kit came out, so you switched. Code needs the same kind of record: a file format changes, so you update your code to read it you find a bug, so you fix it you add a feature, and something that used to work stops working Without a system, most of us end up keeping versions by renaming files (Figure 5.1). This works, sort of, until you can’t remember which file is the latest, what changed between v2 and v3_outline_of_reduced_discussion, or whose edits are whose. Things get particularly messy when you collaborate. Figure 5.1: Version control by file name. One manuscript, many versions, two collaborators. A version control system solves this problem properly. Git, written by Linus Torvalds (who also wrote Linux) to manage thousands of programmers working on Linux at the same time, is by far the most popular one. Git lets you: keep snapshots of your project, so you can trace the origin of a bug and roll back a bad change trace how your code evolved, and why, which helps make your work reproducible keep your code organized and available after people leave the lab share your code with others and work on it together Git is the standard tool for version control in data science and bioinformatics. Nearly every bioinformatics program you’ll download comes from a Git repository. Further reading. This chapter follows the Git chapter of Vince Buffalo’s Bioinformatics Data Skills (O’Reilly, 2015). For a complete reference, see the free book Pro Git. Both are listed in the References. 5.2 Installing and configuring Git Check whether Git is already installed: git --version If it isn’t, here’s how to install it (more details): System How to install Git Mac Run xcode-select --install (Apple’s command-line tools include Git), or brew install git Linux / WSL sudo apt install git (Ubuntu and Debian) Git commands all take the form git <subcommand>. Before you use Git, tell it who you are. Git records your name and email address with every change you make. You only need to do this once per computer: git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@uark.edu" git config --global init.defaultBranch main # name the first branch "main" git config --global core.editor nano # the editor Git opens for messages git config --global color.ui true # color-coded output git config --list # check your settings --global stores these settings in the file ~/.gitconfig, so they apply to every project on that computer. Use the same email address you use (or will use) for GitHub. Why init.defaultBranch? Every repository starts on a default branch (Section 5.11). Git originally called it master; GitHub and most projects now call it main. Without this setting, Git still uses master and prints a hint every time you create a repository. You’ll see both names in tutorials. They mean the same thing. 5.3 Creating a repository A repository (or repo) is a project directory whose history Git is keeping track of. Let’s make one called bio_project, then turn it into a Git repository with git init: mkdir bio_project cd bio_project git init Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/you/bio_project/.git/ git init creates a hidden directory, .git, where Git stores the entire history of your project: ls -a . .. .git You never need to touch anything inside .git. But don’t delete it: that would delete your project’s history. Don’t make a repository inside another repository. Run git init once, at the top level of a project. If git status (below) works in a directory where you haven’t run git init, you’re already inside a repository. 5.4 Track, stage, commit Figure 5.2 shows how Git works. Files in your project directory (the working directory) are either untracked (Git ignores them) or tracked (Git is watching them). When you’ve made changes worth keeping, you git add them to the staging area, and then git commit stores a permanent snapshot of everything that’s staged in your local repository. Later in the chapter, you’ll git push your commits to a remote repository on GitHub. Figure 5.2: The Git workflow. git add starts tracking a file and stages its changes; git commit stores the staged changes in the repository; git push and git pull send and receive commits from a remote repository. 5.4.1 Checking the status of your files Let’s add some files to bio_project. The touch command creates empty files: mkdir data touch README data/README data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta git status On branch main No commits yet Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) README data/ nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track) git status is the command you’ll use most. It tells you which branch you’re on (main, the default), what’s happened since your last commit, and often what to do next. Right now Git sees some new files and a new directory, but it isn’t tracking any of them. 5.4.2 Tracking files with git add git add tells Git to start tracking files: git add README data/README git status On branch main No commits yet Changes to be committed: (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage) new file: README new file: data/README Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta The two README files are now tracked, and their current versions are staged: they’ll be included in the next commit. The FASTA files are still untracked. 5.4.3 Staging changes with git add Now let’s change README: echo "The README file for my project" >> README git status On branch main No commits yet Changes to be committed: (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage) new file: README new file: data/README Changes not staged for commit: (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed) (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory) modified: README Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta README now appears twice: once under Changes to be committed and once under Changes not staged for commit. That’s because Git staged a snapshot of README when we ran git add, before we added that line. If we commit now, the commit will hold the empty README, not the new version. To include the new line, stage README again: git add README git status On branch main No commits yet Changes to be committed: (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage) new file: README new file: data/README Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta So git add does two things: starts tracking a file that Git isn’t tracking yet stages the current changes to a file that Git is already tracking Changes are staged as they were when you ran git add. Anything you change after git add isn’t included in the next commit unless you git add the file again. git status tells you when that’s the case. 5.4.4 Storing changes with git commit git commit stores a snapshot of everything that’s staged, along with a message that describes the change: git commit -m "Initial import" git status [main (root-commit) 430362b] Initial import 2 files changed, 1 insertion(+) create mode 100644 README create mode 100644 data/README On branch main Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track) That’s it: the two README files are safely stored in the repository. The seven characters after main (and root-commit, meaning this is the first commit) are the start of the commit’s ID. Git computes a unique ID for every commit from its contents (a SHA-1 checksum, like the ones in Section 4.5). Your IDs will differ from the ones in this book. If you leave off -m "message", Git opens your editor so you can write the message there. Save and exit, and Git makes the commit. Why have a staging area at all? You’ll often be working on several files at once. Some changes will be finished, others not. Staging lets you choose exactly which changes go into each commit, so each commit is a meaningful step in your project (“Fix the GC-content calculation”) rather than a random snapshot of everything you happened to be working on. Writing good commit messages Your commit messages are the history of your project. Six months from now, “Fix off-by-one error in exon coordinates” will mean something; “stuff” will not (Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3: Commit messages over the life of a project. xkcd.com/1296, CC BY-NC 2.5. Write a short summary, about 50 characters or less, that says what the commit does: “Add GC-content function”, “Fix crash on empty FASTA files”. Commit often, in small, related chunks. One commit, one idea. Don’t commit broken code to main if you can help it. That’s what branches are for (Section 5.11). 5.5 Undoing changes Let’s add a line to README and stage it: echo "Wrote the best script of my life" >> README git add README git status On branch main Changes to be committed: (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage) modified: README Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta Changed your mind? Git tells you how to unstage the file with git restore --staged: git restore --staged README git status On branch main Changes not staged for commit: (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed) (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory) modified: README Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a") The change is no longer staged, but it’s still in the file. To throw the change away entirely and put the file back the way it was at the last commit, use git restore without --staged: git restore README cat README git status The README file for my project On branch main Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) data/sample1.fasta data/sample2.fasta nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track) git restore file can’t be undone. It overwrites your file with the version from the last commit. Any changes you hadn’t committed are gone for good, just as with rm. git checkout and git reset. git restore (and git switch, below) arrived in 2019. Older tutorials, and Stack Overflow, do the same things with git checkout -- file (discard changes) and git reset HEAD file (unstage). Both still work. 5.6 Ignoring files with .gitignore git status keeps reminding us that the FASTA files aren’t being tracked. Suppose we don’t want them in the repository: they’re large and can be downloaded again. List the files Git should ignore, one pattern per line, in a file called .gitignore at the top of the repository: echo 'data/*.fasta' > .gitignore git status On branch main Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) .gitignore nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track) The FASTA files have disappeared from the list. .gitignore itself is a file worth keeping, so commit it: git add .gitignore git commit -m "Ignore FASTA files in data/" git status [main 054b92e] Ignore FASTA files in data/ 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) create mode 100644 .gitignore On branch main nothing to commit, working tree clean Working tree clean means everything in the directory is either committed or ignored. Here’s a typical .gitignore for a bioinformatics project: # large data and results: keep these out of the repository data/ results/ *.fastq.gz *.bam # junk your computer makes .DS_Store __pycache__/ .Rproj.user/ .Rhistory Keep big data files out of Git. Git is built for text files such as code, notes, and small tables. It keeps every version of every file forever, so large data files bloat your repository. GitHub won’t accept files larger than 100 MB. Back up data separately, and keep the commands that download or generate it (Section 4.3) in the repository instead. 5.7 Viewing history with git log Let’s make one more commit: echo "Project started 2026-01-14" >> README git add README git commit -m "Add project start date" [main c5ae50e] Add project start date 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) git log lists the commits, newest first: git log commit c5ae50eed76e4e8f9c2daa082fa4d000ce924f97 Author: Andrew Alverson <aja@uark.edu> Date: Mon Nov 2 22:29:42 2026 -0600 Add project start date commit 054b92ec05ffd82d87ff23d27ea6782e4e85a568 Author: Andrew Alverson <aja@uark.edu> Date: Mon Nov 2 22:29:42 2026 -0600 Ignore FASTA files in data/ commit 430362bab283438e5268bb005f11c6a11f34c8da Author: Andrew Alverson <aja@uark.edu> Date: Mon Nov 2 22:29:42 2026 -0600 Initial import Each commit has a full 40-character ID, an author, a date, and the commit message. A few useful options: git log --oneline c5ae50e Add project start date 054b92e Ignore FASTA files in data/ 430362b Initial import git log --name-status -n 2 commit c5ae50eed76e4e8f9c2daa082fa4d000ce924f97 Author: Andrew Alverson <aja@uark.edu> Date: Mon Nov 2 22:29:42 2026 -0600 Add project start date M README commit 054b92ec05ffd82d87ff23d27ea6782e4e85a568 Author: Andrew Alverson <aja@uark.edu> Date: Mon Nov 2 22:29:42 2026 -0600 Ignore FASTA files in data/ A .gitignore --oneline gives one short line per commit, --name-status lists the files each commit changed (A added, M modified, D deleted, R renamed), and -n 2 shows only the two most recent commits. 5.8 Seeing what changed with git diff git diff shows exactly what you’ve changed. Add a line to README: echo "Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville" >> README git diff diff --git a/README b/README index 62debb3..078409c 100644 --- a/README +++ b/README @@ -1,2 +1,3 @@ The README file for my project Project started 2026-01-14 +Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville The format is similar to diff -u (Section 1.10.7): --- a/README is the old version and +++ b/README is the new one. @@ -1,2 +1,3 @@ says which lines are shown: lines 1–2 of the old version and lines 1–3 of the new one. Lines that start with + were added, lines that start with - were deleted, and lines that start with a space are unchanged context. A line that you edited shows up as a deleted line followed by an added line. By default, git diff compares your working directory to the staging area, which shows changes you haven’t staged yet. What happens after git add? git add README git diff Nothing, because there are no unstaged changes left. To see what’s staged and about to be committed, use git diff --staged: git diff --staged git commit -m "Add sampling location" diff --git a/README b/README index 62debb3..078409c 100644 --- a/README +++ b/README @@ -1,2 +1,3 @@ The README file for my project Project started 2026-01-14 +Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville [main 3164e02] Add sampling location 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) 5.9 Renaming and deleting files If you rename or delete a tracked file with mv or rm, Git sees the old file as deleted and the new file as untracked. Do it Git’s way instead, with git mv and git rm, which make the change and stage it in one step. Let’s give the README files a .md extension, which tells GitHub that they’re written in Markdown (Section 5.12.5): git mv README README.md git mv data/README data/README.md git status On branch main Changes to be committed: (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage) renamed: README -> README.md renamed: data/README -> data/README.md git commit -m "Add Markdown extension to README files" [main f3028ea] Add Markdown extension to README files 2 files changed, 0 insertions(+), 0 deletions(-) rename README => README.md (100%) rename data/{README => README.md} (100%) git rm file deletes a file and stages the deletion. git rm --cached file stops tracking a file but leaves it on your computer, which is handy when you committed a file by mistake and want to add it to .gitignore. 5.10 Retrieving an old version This is where version control earns its keep. Let’s make a change we’ll come to regret: echo "TODO: delete all the raw data" >> README.md git commit -am "Update README" git log --oneline [main ac0c0bf] Update README 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) ac0c0bf Update README f3028ea Add Markdown extension to README files 3164e02 Add sampling location c5ae50e Add project start date 054b92e Ignore FASTA files in data/ 430362b Initial import git commit -a stages every change to tracked files before committing, so you can skip git add. It never adds untracked files. Use it only when you know what you’ve changed. To view an old version of a file without changing anything, use git show commit:file. Instead of a commit ID, you can count back from the most recent commit, which Git calls HEAD: HEAD~1 is one commit before, HEAD~2 is two before, and so on. git show HEAD~1:README.md The README file for my project Project started 2026-01-14 Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville To get that version back, restore the file from that commit: git restore --source=HEAD~1 README.md cat README.md git status The README file for my project Project started 2026-01-14 Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville On branch main Changes not staged for commit: (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed) (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory) modified: README.md no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a") The old version is now in your working directory, as a change you can commit: git commit -am "Remove bad advice from README" [main db313a2] Remove bad advice from README 1 file changed, 1 deletion(-) The bad version is still in the history, in case you ever want it back. That’s the point: once you’ve committed something, it’s very hard to lose. You can use a commit ID in place of HEAD~1, for example git restore --source=4f2a9c1 README.md. Branches let you try something new (a major new feature, a different way of doing an analysis) without any risk of breaking the version on main that works. If the experiment works out, you merge it back into main. If it doesn’t, you abandon the branch and main is unscathed. Collaborators can each work on their own branch and merge their work in when it’s ready. Figure 5.4: Working on a branch. You create a branch from main and make commits on it, while main carries on. When the work is done, you merge it back into main. Branches are cheap: Git doesn’t copy your files to make one, so creating and switching branches is instant. 5.11.1 Creating, switching, and merging git branch lists the branches, with a * next to the one you’re on. Let’s make a new branch called readme-changes and switch to it: git branch readme-changes git branch git switch readme-changes git branch * main readme-changes Switched to branch 'readme-changes' main * readme-changes Now make a change and commit it on readme-changes: echo "Data are in data/, one FASTA file per sample." >> README.md git commit -am "Describe the data directory" git log --oneline -n 3 [readme-changes 5af8ca4] Describe the data directory 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) 5af8ca4 Describe the data directory db313a2 Remove bad advice from README ac0c0bf Update README The new commit exists only on readme-changes. If you switch back to main, the new line disappears from README.md: git switch main tail -n 2 README.md Switched to branch 'main' Project started 2026-01-14 Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville It’s not gone. It’s on the other branch. To bring it into main, switch to the branch you want to merge into (main, which we just did) and then merge the other branch: git merge readme-changes tail -n 2 README.md Updating db313a2..5af8ca4 Fast-forward README.md | 1 + 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville Data are in data/, one FASTA file per sample. Because main hadn’t changed since we created the branch, Git simply moved main forward to include the new commit, a fast-forward merge. If both branches have new commits, Git combines them in a new merge commit, as in Figure 5.4. Once a branch is merged, you can delete it: git branch -d readme-changes Deleted branch readme-changes (was 5af8ca4). Create and switch in one step. git switch -c new-branch creates a branch and switches to it. (In older tutorials: git checkout -b new-branch.) 5.11.2 Merge conflicts Git can merge changes to different files, or to different parts of the same file, on its own. But if two branches change the same lines of a file, Git can’t know which version you want. That’s a merge conflict, and you have to resolve it yourself. Conflicts sound scary, but they’re routine. Let’s make one. On a new branch, change the first line of README.md and commit: git switch -c new-title nano README.md # change the first line git diff git commit -am "Shorter title" diff --git a/README.md b/README.md index 3bad163..d478709 100644 --- a/README.md +++ b/README.md @@ -1,4 +1,4 @@ -The README file for my project +# bio_project Project started 2026-01-14 Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville Data are in data/, one FASTA file per sample. [new-title cb2edbd] Shorter title 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-) Meanwhile, back on main, we change the same line differently: git switch main nano README.md # change the first line git diff git commit -am "Better title" diff --git a/README.md b/README.md index 3bad163..28da5e8 100644 --- a/README.md +++ b/README.md @@ -1,4 +1,4 @@ -The README file for my project +# Diatom genomics project Project started 2026-01-14 Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville Data are in data/, one FASTA file per sample. [main e462853] Better title 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-) Now merge new-title into main: git merge new-title Auto-merging README.md CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result. Git merged what it could and stopped at the conflict. git status lists the files that need attention: git status On branch main You have unmerged paths. (fix conflicts and run "git commit") (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge) Unmerged paths: (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution) both modified: README.md no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a") Git marked the conflict inside the file: cat README.md <<<<<<< HEAD # Diatom genomics project ======= # bio_project >>>>>>> new-title Project started 2026-01-14 Samples collected from Lake Fayetteville Data are in data/, one FASTA file per sample. The lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= are the version on the branch you’re on (main). The lines between ======= and >>>>>>> new-title are the version from the other branch. To resolve the conflict: Open the file in your editor. Edit it so it says what you want. That might be one version, the other, or a combination. Delete the three marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>). Stage the file with git add and commit. nano README.md # fix the conflict and delete the markers head -n 1 README.md git add README.md git commit -m "Merge new-title, keeping the longer title" git log --oneline --graph # Diatom genomics project [main dfe54ae] Merge new-title, keeping the longer title * dfe54ae Merge new-title, keeping the longer title |\ | * cb2edbd Shorter title * | e462853 Better title |/ * 5af8ca4 Describe the data directory * db313a2 Remove bad advice from README * ac0c0bf Update README * f3028ea Add Markdown extension to README files * 3164e02 Add sampling location * c5ae50e Add project start date * 054b92e Ignore FASTA files in data/ * 430362b Initial import git log --graph draws the history of the branches and the merge commit that joins them, just like Figure 5.4. Changed your mind? In the middle of a conflicted merge, git merge --abort puts everything back the way it was before you ran git merge. A remote repository is a copy of your repository hosted somewhere else, usually on a service such as GitHub (others include GitLab and Bitbucket). A remote repository: backs up your work: if your laptop dies, your code and its entire history are safe shares your work: anyone can see your public repositories (this course’s materials are on GitHub) lets you collaborate: everyone works in their own local repository and exchanges commits through the shared remote Git is a distributed version control system: every copy of a repository contains the full history of the project, and every collaborator can work, commit, and look through the history without a network connection. You only need the network to exchange commits: git push sends your new commits to the remote. git pull fetches new commits from the remote and merges them into your local repository. git clone copies a remote repository, and its entire history, to your computer. Figure 5.5 shows how this works for seqtk, a popular toolkit for working with FASTA and FASTQ files. Its author, Heng Li, pushes his changes to GitHub, where a collaborator clones the repository (A). When the collaborator pushes a change, Heng Li can pull it into his own copy (B). The history on GitHub is a mix of commits from Heng Li and everyone else who contributes.
