Many bioinformatics programs are installed this way: clone the repository, then build the program by following its README. To get the author’s latest changes later, run git pull inside the directory. 5.12.2 Setting up GitHub Create an account at github.com. Pick a professional username: it will appear in the URL of everything you share. Students can also apply for the free GitHub Education benefits. Set up authentication. GitHub doesn’t accept your account password when you push from the command line. Use one of these instead. Option 1: SSH keys (recommended). If you made an SSH key in Section 4.7, you can use the same key for GitHub. Print your public key and copy it: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub On GitHub, go to Settings > SSH and GPG keys > New SSH key, paste it in, and save. Then test the connection: ssh -T git@github.com Hi yourname! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access. With SSH, use the repository’s SSH URL, which looks like git@github.com:yourname/bio_project.git. Option 2: HTTPS with a personal access token. A token is a long, random password that you create on GitHub, at Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens (instructions). Give it an expiration date and only the access it needs (for a fine-grained token, Contents: Read and write on your repositories). Copy the token right away: GitHub shows it only once. When Git asks for your password, paste the token. On a Mac, Git saves it in your Keychain so you don’t have to paste it every time. With HTTPS, use URLs like https://github.com/yourname/bio_project.git. Treat a token like a password. Anyone with your token can do whatever the token allows to your GitHub account. Don’t put it in a script, email it, or commit it to a repository. If one leaks, delete it on GitHub and make a new one. Working on the cluster? Git works the same way on the cluster. To push from there, make an SSH key on the cluster with ssh-keygen and add that public key to GitHub too. You can add as many keys as you like, one per computer. 5.12.3 Pushing a local repository to GitHub To put bio_project on GitHub: On GitHub, click + (top right) > New repository. Name it bio_project. Choose public or private. Don’t add a README, .gitignore, or license. We already have a repository with its own history, so the one on GitHub should start out empty. Click Create repository. GitHub shows the commands you need, with your repository’s URL filled in. Back in the Terminal, inside bio_project, tell your local repository about the remote. By convention, the main remote is named origin: git remote add origin git@github.com:yourname/bio_project.git git remote -v # check it origin git@github.com:yourname/bio_project.git (fetch) origin git@github.com:yourname/bio_project.git (push) Then push. The first time, -u origin main links your local main branch to main on GitHub, so later you can simply type git push and git pull: git push -u origin main Enumerating objects: 26, done. Refresh the repository’s page on GitHub: your files, commit messages, and history are all there. 5.12.4 The everyday workflow Once a project is on GitHub, a typical working session looks like this: git pull # get any changes made elsewhere # ... work on your files ... git status # what did I change? git add script.py notes.md # stage the changes you want to keep git commit -m "Add GC-content function" git push # back up and share If you work on more than one computer (say, your laptop and the cluster), always git pull before you start and git push when you’re done. If a collaborator pushed changes to the same lines you changed, git pull reports a merge conflict, which you resolve exactly as in Section 5.11.2, and then push. git push is rejected? If GitHub has commits that you don’t have yet, git push refuses with a message about the remote containing work that you don’t have locally. Run git pull first, resolve any conflicts, and push again. 5.12.5 README files and Markdown GitHub displays a repository’s README.md on its front page, so it’s the first thing visitors read. Use it to explain what the project is, how to run the code, and where the data come from. README files are written in Markdown (Section 3.6). GitHub formats Markdown files wherever they appear in a repository, so your data/README.md (Section 3.3) is nicely formatted, too.
